<result># SCIP and monokl: Research Verdict

## 1. Schema (primary source: `scip.proto`, fetched directly from the repo)

Core messages, verified from the actual `.proto` file ([scip.proto](https://github.com/sourcegraph/scip/blob/main/scip.proto)):

- **`Index`**: `metadata`, `repeated Document documents`, `repeated SymbolInformation external_symbols` (for symbols referenced but defined outside this index).
- **`Document`**: `language`, `relative_path` (root-relative, canonical, `/`-separated), `repeated Occurrence occurrences`, `repeated SymbolInformation symbols`, optional `text`, `position_encoding`.
- **`SymbolInformation`**: `symbol` (string), `documentation[]`, `relationships[]`, `kind` (a 110+-value enum: Class/Trait/Struct/Method/… with language-specific entries like Rust's `Trait`/`TraitMethod`), `display_name`, `signature_documentation`, `enclosing_symbol`.
- **`Occurrence`**: a range (typed `SingleLineRange`/`MultiLineRange` oneof, superseding a deprecated packed-int encoding), `symbol`, `symbol_roles` (bitset: Definition/Import/WriteAccess/ReadAccess/Generated/Test/ForwardDefinition), `syntax_kind`, `diagnostics[]`, `enclosing_range`.
- **`Relationship`**: `symbol`, plus four booleans (`is_reference`, `is_implementation`, `is_type_definition`, `is_definition`).

Notably, there is **no confidence/precision field anywhere** — SCIP has nothing analogous to monokl's `CapabilityPrecision`.

## 2. Moniker grammar

Verbatim from `scip.proto`: `<symbol> ::= <scheme> ' ' <package> ' ' (<descriptor>)+ | 'local ' <local-id>`, `<package> ::= <manager> ' ' <package-name> ' ' <version>`, with descriptors for namespace(`/`), type(`#`), term(`.`), method(`(disambiguator).`), type-parameter(`[]`), parameter(`()`), meta(`:`), macro(`!`). Crucially, `manager`/`package-name`/`version` each explicitly permit `.` as an "empty" placeholder. Real managers in practice: `npm` (scip-typescript), `maven` (scip-java/scip-semanticdb, per [scip-java docs](https://github.com/sourcegraph/scip-java/blob/main/docs/design.md)).

**Fit for monokl**: less baggage than it first looks — package resolution isn't mandatory (`.` placeholders exist precisely for this). But the full grammar (backtick-escaping, method disambiguators, suffix taxonomy) is real string-parsing surface that buys monokl nothing over its existing `(FileIdx, usize)`/name-string keys, which are cheaper and don't need serialization rules at all.

## 3. Relationship — real vs. paper

The proto's own worked example (TypeScript `Animal`/`Dog`) shows exactly monokl's trait-impl use case: `Dog#` gets `relationships = [{symbol: "Animal#", is_implementation: true}]`. On paper this generalizes cleanly to Override/TypeOf/Reference kinds beyond just trait-impls.

**But**: I checked the actual Rust producer. In `rust-analyzer`'s SCIP CLI (`crates/rust-analyzer/src/cli/scip.rs`, `compute_symbol_info`, fetched from `rust-lang/rust-analyzer` master), the field is hardcoded: `relationships: Vec::new()`. Today's rust-analyzer SCIP output carries **zero** implementation/override relationships. So for monokl's specific first target — Rust trait impls — there is no real SCIP data to consume yet, even though rust-analyzer is the de facto "scip-rust."

## 4. Indexer maturity

- **scip-typescript** ([repo](https://github.com/sourcegraph/scip-typescript)): active — v0.4.0 released Oct 2025, 327 commits, 18 releases, 10 open issues/44 PRs.
- **scip-python** ([repo](https://github.com/sourcegraph/scip-python)): a pyright fork with "no substantial changes to pyright library," developed on its `scip` branch; recent v0.6.3 fixed an inheritance/decorator crash and a macOS zero-document bug — maintained, narrower team.
- **scip-java** ([repo](https://github.com/sourcegraph/scip-java)): javac/scalac compiler-plugin based, covers Java/Scala/Kotlin (with [scip-kotlin](https://github.com/sourcegraph/scip-kotlin)); 775 commits, 30 contributors per [Scaladex](https://index.scala-lang.org/sourcegraph/scip-java), PR activity through Sept–Oct 2025 — the most heavily invested indexer.
- **scip-go** ([repo](https://github.com/sourcegraph/scip-go)): exists, actively maintained.
- **scip-rust**: no standalone project; `rust-analyzer scip <path> --output index.scip` is the built-in indexer, listed in SCIP's own README under "Tools using SCIP."
- **Governance**: as of March 2026 Sourcegraph transitioned SCIP to independent governance — a Core Steering Committee with Meta and Uber engineers alongside Sourcegraph, plus a formal SEP RFC process ([announcement](https://sourcegraph.com/blog/the-future-of-scip)) — real cross-org backing, not vaporware.

## 5. Consumption precedent, and Rust cost

Sourcegraph's own model is **CI-precomputed, not live**: indexers run in CI, emit `index.scip`, then `src code-intel upload`/`src lsif upload` pushes it once ([docs](https://docs.sourcegraph.com/code_navigation/how-to/adding_lsif_to_workflows)). Real third-party consumption exists: **Meta's Glean** ingests Sourcegraph's scip-python output via a cargo-installable "scip-to-glean" converter rather than writing its own Python semantic indexer ([Glean docs](https://glean.software/docs/indexer/scip-python/); [engineering.fb.com](https://engineering.fb.com/2024/12/19/developer-tools/glean-open-source-code-indexing/)). **Mozilla's Searchfox** (mozsearch) consumes scip-java for Java/Kotlin support alongside its own from-scratch indexer ([PR #667](https://github.com/mozsearch/mozsearch/pull/667); [KDAB](https://www.kdab.com/searchfox-improvements/)). Both are genuine "consume SCIP as a supplementary source" precedents, not just theory.

Rust cost is low: an official `scip` crate (v0.9.0, Apache-2.0, [crates.io](https://crates.io/crates/scip)) lives in the SCIP repo's `bindings/rust`, with a single real dependency, `protobuf = "=3.7.2"` (confirmed from its `Cargo.toml`). Parsing is trivial; the hard part is semantic merging — mapping `relative_path`→`FileIdx` and SCIP symbol strings→monokl's local identity, plus reconciling two incompatible `kind`/precision models.

## 6. Should monokl emit SCIP?

Adoption outside Sourcegraph/Meta/Mozilla is thin: **GitLab still has no native SCIP support**, only a conversion-to-LSIF path, despite an open feature request ([issue #412981](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/issues/412981)). Every real producer/consumer pair found is a heavyweight, compiler-backed indexer (javac, pyright, tsc, rustc). monokl's regex+import-binding refs are self-admittedly Heuristic; SCIP has no field to express that, so honest emission means either silently overclaiming precision or dropping low-confidence data.

## Recommendations

1. **Borrow the Relationship shape, not the wire format**: generalize `TraitImplIndex` into an internal enum mirroring `is_implementation`/`is_type_definition`/`is_reference`/`is_definition` on (symbol, related-symbol) pairs. Free naming-compatibility insurance; costs nothing today.
2. **Don't replace `(FileIdx, usize)` with SCIP monikers.** Keep monokl's cheap internal keys; only add a narrow, one-directional SCIP-symbol *exporter* (using `.` placeholders) if/when external interop is actually needed.
3. **Treat `.scip` as an optional, batch-precomputed upgrade path**, not a dependency: add an optional reader (via the `scip` crate) that, when a `.scip` file already exists in-repo, promotes matching occurrences from Heuristic to Structural/Exact — but don't invoke `rust-analyzer scip` live, and don't expect it to solve trait-impls yet (it emits no relationships today).
4. **Don't emit SCIP as a monokl output format now** — SCIP's schema has no honest place for Heuristic-tier results, and real non-Sourcegraph adoption is still limited to a handful of well-resourced orgs.</result>

2. Key Technical Concepts:
   - Two-level architecture: `LanguageAnalyzer` (per-file, produces owned `FileAnalysis`) + `WorkspaceEnricher` (folds per-file analyses into `WorkspaceIndex`, containing `ImportGraph` + `SymbolIndex`).
   - Arena lifetime containment (ADR 0002): no OXC `Allocator`-borrowed data may escape a per-file `analyze()` call; everything in `FileAnalysis` must be owned.
   - `CapabilityPrecision` model: `Unsupported < Heuristic < Structural < Exact` — lets different language analyzers report different resolution quality per operation, with `Skipped`/`Warning` diagnostics instead of silent failure/crash.
   - `AnalyzerRegistry` — dispatches files to the first matching `LanguageAnalyzer`; composite `config_hash` for cache invalidation.
   - Two-tier cache: mtime/size fast-path → blake3 `ContentHash` fallback; two storage layers (in-memory `DashMap`, disk-persisted `.monokl/cache.json` version+config-hash gated).
   - 8-stage `search` pipeline: query parse → canonicalize → text prefilter (`grep-searcher`) → boolean eval → block retrieval → BM25 rank (K1=1.5, B=0.5) + node-type/coverage boosts → dedup (>50% line overlap) → token budget (tiktoken o200k_base, 2MB hard cap).
   - `TraitImplEnricher`/`TraitImplIndex` — new design (added to spec) for a reverse "who implements this trait" index, modeled on rust-analyzer's `trait_impls_in_crate_query` and rustdoc's implementors-list generation; composes with `SymbolIndex`/`ImportGraph` via a hardened, capped BFS (enqueue-time `FxHashSet` visited-set, explicit depth limit, cap checked at every push site, `TraversalCapExceeded`/`TraversalReport` instead of silent truncation).
   - `cache_tiers::lookup_or_parse` — newly extracted shared helper (parameterized over `from_persisted`/`cached_is_valid`/`parse` closures) unifying `TsAnalyzer`/`RustAnalyzer`'s previously-duplicated 4-tier cache skeleton.
   - `MonoklError` (thiserror-based, `#[non_exhaustive]`) — variants: `Io`, `Walk`, `RegexBuild`, `NonUtf8Path`, `TooManyTerms`, `TokenizerInit`, `Json`, `PathOutsideRoot`, `StaleDiskCache`, `InvalidGitRef`, `Git`, `SymlinkRejected`, `FileTooLarge`, `LockPoisoned` (all now correctly declared after fixes; `Parse`/`Query` removed as dead code).
   - `LanguageAnalyzer` trait (now complete): `language_id() -> LanguageId`, `supports()`, `capabilities() -> AnalyzerCapabilities`, `analyze_with_profile()`, with `analyze()` as a default method delegating to `analyze_with_profile(..., AnalysisProfile::Full)`.
   - `LanguageId` enum: `TypeScript, Rust, Python, Go, Java` (no CSharp — dropped per roadmap decision).
   - `LangData` enum (`#[non_exhaustive]`, serde tag="language"/content="data"): `Ts, Rust, Python, Go, Java` (CSharp variant removed/replaced).
   - `AnalysisProfile` enum: `Dependencies, Structural, Full`.
   - BM25 tuning (K1=1.5, B=0.5), rounding to 6 decimals for cross-platform determinism.
   - Non-goals (documented in PRINCIPLES.md): no persistent search index, no full Salsa (yet — open track), no embedding-based retrieval by default, no stemming, no in-memory trigram index (rejected: measured 600MB-1.2GB), no tree-sitter for TS/JS (OXC instead), no running agent loop.
   - Native parser landscape per language: TS/JS = OXC (native Rust, adopted); Rust = `ra_ap_syntax` (kept over `syn` — syn's fail-fast parsing is a real regression for scanning WIP/broken code); Python = tree-sitter-python (Ruff's Rust-native crates rejected as unstable); Go = `gosyn` (real, viable native Rust parser — the standout finding); Java = tree-sitter-java (no viable native Rust parser exists).
   - `oxc_semantic` — recommended addition for TS/JS scope-aware reference resolution (lockstep-versioned, same arena discipline as existing OXC deps).
   - `ra_ap_hir` / Salsa — real Rust semantic resolution capability, but daemon-only cost model; Salsa flagged as an independent, lighter investigation track (real precedent: Astral's `ty`/red-knot, Biome) decoupled from the `ra_ap_hir`-needs-a-daemon question.
   - SCIP (Sourcegraph Code Intelligence Protocol) — currently under active research (background agent still running) for potential relevance to monokl's symbol identity/relationship modeling and possible output-format or ingestion strategy.
   - Eval harness design (recommended, not yet built): two-layer — deterministic retrieval eval (RepoBench-R/CodeSearchNet-style recall@k/MRR) + agent A/B (model/effort pinned, ≥5 runs/condition median+IQR, ≥10 repos frozen task list, report token AND dollar cost separately, broken out by cache-read vs fresh-input mix).
   - Rust workspace clippy lint policy: deny `unwrap_used`, `expect_used`, `panic`, `unreachable`, `unimplemented`, `dbg_macro`, `todo` in lib code (allowed only in `#[cfg(test)]`); `unsafe_code = "deny"`.
   - `camino::Utf8Path`/`Utf8PathBuf` used everywhere instead of `std::path::Path`; `rustc-hash::FxHashMap`/`FxHashSet` for hot-path maps; `BTreeMap` for anything serialized to JSON (deterministic key order).
   - RTK (Rust Token Killer) — user's global bash-command proxy (per their global CLAUDE.md) that summarizes/truncates verbose bash output for token savings; occasionally produces misleading summarized output (e.g. "[N more lines]" instead of real `head` output) requiring the Read tool for precision instead.

# Agent guidance

Guidance for AI coding agents working in this repo. Vendor-neutral — see
[CLAUDE.md](CLAUDE.md) for Claude Code-specific additions.

## Read this first

1. [`docs/spec/README.md`](docs/spec/README.md) — index of the full spec, tells you which file
   covers what.
2. [`docs/spec/05-research-and-decisions.md`](docs/spec/05-research-and-decisions.md) — the
   changelog. If something in files 01-04 looks inconsistent, check here before "fixing" it;
   it's probably already addressed, and the reasoning is recorded.
3. [PRINCIPLES.md](PRINCIPLES.md) — non-goals in particular. Don't propose an embedding-based
   reranker, a persistent trigram index, or a tree-sitter TS/JS parser — all three were
   considered and explicitly rejected, with reasons on record.

## Current state

No code exists yet — this is spec-stage. There's no `Cargo.toml`, no build, no test suite to
run. If you're asked to implement something, you're implementing *from* the spec, not
extending existing code. Don't invent APIs, types, or command flags that aren't in the spec
without flagging that you're doing so — the spec is meant to be reconstructed verbatim, and
silent deviation defeats that.

## Code conventions (apply from the first line of code)

- No `unwrap()`/`expect()`/`panic!()`/`unreachable!()`/`unimplemented!()` outside
  `#[cfg(test)]` — denied by the workspace's own clippy lint table.
- One `thiserror` error enum per crate. Compose new failure modes via `#[from]`/`#[source]`,
  don't add a `String`-message variant when a structured one is possible.
- `LanguageAnalyzer` implementations must return fully owned data — no arena-borrowed AST
  nodes, no lifetimes tied to the parser's `Allocator`, ever, in any field of `FileAnalysis`.
- `camino::Utf8Path`/`Utf8PathBuf` everywhere paths appear — not `std::path::Path`.
- `rustc-hash`'s `FxHashMap`/`FxHashSet` for hot-path internal maps; `BTreeMap` for anything
  that gets serialized to JSON output (stable key order is load-bearing for determinism, see
  [PRINCIPLES.md](PRINCIPLES.md)).

## When you find a real bug in the spec

Fix it in the spec file, and add an entry to
[`docs/spec/05-research-and-decisions.md`](docs/spec/05-research-and-decisions.md) explaining
what was wrong and why the fix is correct — the same pattern already used for the two
compile-breaking gaps found there. Don't fix it only in code without updating the spec; the
spec is the reconstruction source, and a silent divergence between the two is worse than either
one being wrong on its own.

## Testing

`cargo nextest` once tests exist. `insta` for snapshots — accept a snapshot change only after
confirming the new output is actually correct, not just different.

# Contributing

## Where things stand

monokl is spec-stage — no `Cargo.toml`, no `src/`, nothing to build or run yet. The design is
fully written up in [`docs/spec/`](docs/spec/README.md). If you're picking this up to start
implementation, read [`docs/spec/README.md`](docs/spec/README.md) first; it tells you which
file to read for which subsystem.

Before writing code against the spec, check
[`docs/spec/05-research-and-decisions.md`](docs/spec/05-research-and-decisions.md) — it's the
changelog for corrections made after the fact (compile-breaking gaps, dropped languages,
adopted-but-unbuilt design changes). The other four spec files are the source of truth for *what*
to build; this one is the source of truth for *why* it looks the way it does.

## Proposing a spec change

Don't silently edit around a design decision you disagree with. Add a dated entry to
`docs/spec/05-research-and-decisions.md` explaining what changed and why — same discipline
that's already been applied throughout that file. If the change is substantial enough to need
its own writeup, add a new file under `docs/spec/` and link it from
[`docs/spec/README.md`](docs/spec/README.md).

## Once there's code

These conventions are already locked into the spec — `docs/spec/01-core-architecture.md`'s
workspace lint table — and apply from the first commit, not as an aspiration to grow into:

- **No `unwrap()`, `expect()`, `panic!()`, `unreachable!()`, or `unimplemented!()` in library
  code.** Denied at the workspace level via `clippy`. Fine in `#[cfg(test)]` code — assertions
  are supposed to panic on failure there.
- **`thiserror`, one error enum per crate**, composed via `#[from]`/`#[source]` rather than
  proliferating string-message variants. See `MonoklError` in
  [`docs/spec/01-core-architecture.md`](docs/spec/01-core-architecture.md) for the pattern.
- **Arena data never escapes a per-file parse call.** If you're touching a `LanguageAnalyzer`
  impl, everything in the returned `FileAnalysis` must be owned — no borrowed AST nodes, no
  lifetimes tied to the parser's allocator.
- **`camino::Utf8Path`/`Utf8PathBuf`**, not `std::path::Path` — the whole crate assumes UTF-8
  paths.
- **`cargo nextest`** for running tests, **`insta`** for snapshot tests.

## Filing an issue

Say what you expected, what happened, and — if it's a spec-vs-reality mismatch — which file in
`docs/spec/` you were reading. "The spec says X but Y happens" is more actionable than "this is
broken."

**In Claude Code:** Use the `Skill` tool. When you invoke a skill, its content is loaded and presented to you—follow it directly. Never use the Read tool on skill files.

**In other environments:** Check your platform's documentation for how skills are loaded.

We should do this:

❯ Any other projects, research we should consider for inspiration?

Yes — a few genuinely unexplored pieces of prior art that are closer analogs to monokl than anything researched so far:

- GitHub's stack-graphs (https://github.com/github/stack-graphs) + tree-sitter-graph — a Rust library purpose-built for scope-based name resolution across languages, without a full type-checker. This directly targets the exact problem that kept coming up (TS reference resolution, Rust's heuristic module-path walker, Python/Go/Java all lacking a cheap-but-real resolution tier) — worth checking whether it's a better general answer than solving it per-language.
- ast-grep (https://ast-grep.github.io/) — Rust-native, tree-sitter-based structural search with its own query DSL. This is architecturally the closest sibling to monokl of anything examined yet (closer than codegraph, which is TypeScript). Worth studying its query-language design and how it handles less-invested languages.
- difftastic (https://difftast.icl/) — Rust-native, tree-sitter-based structural diff, same author has written good engineering material on tree-sitter performance tradeoffs in Rust. Directly relevant since monokl already specs a diff command.
- The call-graph/points-to analysis literature (CHA, RTA, k-CFA) — I flagged this as high-value two turns ago when you asked about backing the work with established science, but we got pulled into the Rust-idiom audit and doc reorg before actually researching it. Still open.

Lower priority but worth a mention: CodeQL, SCIP/LSIF, Kythe, Glean — decade-old production code-intelligence schemas, only ever cited in passing as "established practice." Actually studying how they structure queries/indices would be good grounding, even if monokl doesn't adopt their schema.

Want me to run research on the top four now?

<result># SCIP and monokl: Research Verdict

## 1. Schema (primary source: `scip.proto`, fetched directly from the repo)

Core messages, verified from the actual `.proto` file ([scip.proto](https://github.com/sourcegraph/scip/blob/main/scip.proto)):

- **`Index`**: `metadata`, `repeated Document documents`, `repeated SymbolInformation external_symbols` (for symbols referenced but defined outside this index).
- **`Document`**: `language`, `relative_path` (root-relative, canonical, `/`-separated), `repeated Occurrence occurrences`, `repeated SymbolInformation symbols`, optional `text`, `position_encoding`.
- **`SymbolInformation`**: `symbol` (string), `documentation[]`, `relationships[]`, `kind` (a 110+-value enum: Class/Trait/Struct/Method/… with language-specific entries like Rust's `Trait`/`TraitMethod`), `display_name`, `signature_documentation`, `enclosing_symbol`.
- **`Occurrence`**: a range (typed `SingleLineRange`/`MultiLineRange` oneof, superseding a deprecated packed-int encoding), `symbol`, `symbol_roles` (bitset: Definition/Import/WriteAccess/ReadAccess/Generated/Test/ForwardDefinition), `syntax_kind`, `diagnostics[]`, `enclosing_range`.
- **`Relationship`**: `symbol`, plus four booleans (`is_reference`, `is_implementation`, `is_type_definition`, `is_definition`).

Notably, there is **no confidence/precision field anywhere** — SCIP has nothing analogous to monokl's `CapabilityPrecision`.

## 2. Moniker grammar

Verbatim from `scip.proto`: `<symbol> ::= <scheme> ' ' <package> ' ' (<descriptor>)+ | 'local ' <local-id>`, `<package> ::= <manager> ' ' <package-name> ' ' <version>`, with descriptors for namespace(`/`), type(`#`), term(`.`), method(`(disambiguator).`), type-parameter(`[]`), parameter(`()`), meta(`:`), macro(`!`). Crucially, `manager`/`package-name`/`version` each explicitly permit `.` as an "empty" placeholder. Real managers in practice: `npm` (scip-typescript), `maven` (scip-java/scip-semanticdb, per [scip-java docs](https://github.com/sourcegraph/scip-java/blob/main/docs/design.md)).

**Fit for monokl**: less baggage than it first looks — package resolution isn't mandatory (`.` placeholders exist precisely for this). But the full grammar (backtick-escaping, method disambiguators, suffix taxonomy) is real string-parsing surface that buys monokl nothing over its existing `(FileIdx, usize)`/name-string keys, which are cheaper and don't need serialization rules at all.

## 3. Relationship — real vs. paper

The proto's own worked example (TypeScript `Animal`/`Dog`) shows exactly monokl's trait-impl use case: `Dog#` gets `relationships = [{symbol: "Animal#", is_implementation: true}]`. On paper this generalizes cleanly to Override/TypeOf/Reference kinds beyond just trait-impls.

**But**: I checked the actual Rust producer. In `rust-analyzer`'s SCIP CLI (`crates/rust-analyzer/src/cli/scip.rs`, `compute_symbol_info`, fetched from `rust-lang/rust-analyzer` master), the field is hardcoded: `relationships: Vec::new()`. Today's rust-analyzer SCIP output carries **zero** implementation/override relationships. So for monokl's specific first target — Rust trait impls — there is no real SCIP data to consume yet, even though rust-analyzer is the de facto "scip-rust."

## 4. Indexer maturity

- **scip-typescript** ([repo](https://github.com/sourcegraph/scip-typescript)): active — v0.4.0 released Oct 2025, 327 commits, 18 releases, 10 open issues/44 PRs.
- **scip-python** ([repo](https://github.com/sourcegraph/scip-python)): a pyright fork with "no substantial changes to pyright library," developed on its `scip` branch; recent v0.6.3 fixed an inheritance/decorator crash and a macOS zero-document bug — maintained, narrower team.
- **scip-java** ([repo](https://github.com/sourcegraph/scip-java)): javac/scalac compiler-plugin based, covers Java/Scala/Kotlin (with [scip-kotlin](https://github.com/sourcegraph/scip-kotlin)); 775 commits, 30 contributors per [Scaladex](https://index.scala-lang.org/sourcegraph/scip-java), PR activity through Sept–Oct 2025 — the most heavily invested indexer.
- **scip-go** ([repo](https://github.com/sourcegraph/scip-go)): exists, actively maintained.
- **scip-rust**: no standalone project; `rust-analyzer scip <path> --output index.scip` is the built-in indexer, listed in SCIP's own README under "Tools using SCIP."
- **Governance**: as of March 2026 Sourcegraph transitioned SCIP to independent governance — a Core Steering Committee with Meta and Uber engineers alongside Sourcegraph, plus a formal SEP RFC process ([announcement](https://sourcegraph.com/blog/the-future-of-scip)) — real cross-org backing, not vaporware.

## 5. Consumption precedent, and Rust cost

Sourcegraph's own model is **CI-precomputed, not live**: indexers run in CI, emit `index.scip`, then `src code-intel upload`/`src lsif upload` pushes it once ([docs](https://docs.sourcegraph.com/code_navigation/how-to/adding_lsif_to_workflows)). Real third-party consumption exists: **Meta's Glean** ingests Sourcegraph's scip-python output via a cargo-installable "scip-to-glean" converter rather than writing its own Python semantic indexer ([Glean docs](https://glean.software/docs/indexer/scip-python/); [engineering.fb.com](https://engineering.fb.com/2024/12/19/developer-tools/glean-open-source-code-indexing/)). **Mozilla's Searchfox** (mozsearch) consumes scip-java for Java/Kotlin support alongside its own from-scratch indexer ([PR #667](https://github.com/mozsearch/mozsearch/pull/667); [KDAB](https://www.kdab.com/searchfox-improvements/)). Both are genuine "consume SCIP as a supplementary source" precedents, not just theory.

Rust cost is low: an official `scip` crate (v0.9.0, Apache-2.0, [crates.io](https://crates.io/crates/scip)) lives in the SCIP repo's `bindings/rust`, with a single real dependency, `protobuf = "=3.7.2"` (confirmed from its `Cargo.toml`). Parsing is trivial; the hard part is semantic merging — mapping `relative_path`→`FileIdx` and SCIP symbol strings→monokl's local identity, plus reconciling two incompatible `kind`/precision models.

## 6. Should monokl emit SCIP?

Adoption outside Sourcegraph/Meta/Mozilla is thin: **GitLab still has no native SCIP support**, only a conversion-to-LSIF path, despite an open feature request ([issue #412981](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/issues/412981)). Every real producer/consumer pair found is a heavyweight, compiler-backed indexer (javac, pyright, tsc, rustc). monokl's regex+import-binding refs are self-admittedly Heuristic; SCIP has no field to express that, so honest emission means either silently overclaiming precision or dropping low-confidence data.

## Recommendations

1. **Borrow the Relationship shape, not the wire format**: generalize `TraitImplIndex` into an internal enum mirroring `is_implementation`/`is_type_definition`/`is_reference`/`is_definition` on (symbol, related-symbol) pairs. Free naming-compatibility insurance; costs nothing today.
2. **Don't replace `(FileIdx, usize)` with SCIP monikers.** Keep monokl's cheap internal keys; only add a narrow, one-directional SCIP-symbol *exporter* (using `.` placeholders) if/when external interop is actually needed.
3. **Treat `.scip` as an optional, batch-precomputed upgrade path**, not a dependency: add an optional reader (via the `scip` crate) that, when a `.scip` file already exists in-repo, promotes matching occurrences from Heuristic to Structural/Exact — but don't invoke `rust-analyzer scip` live, and don't expect it to solve trait-impls yet (it emits no relationships today).
4. **Don't emit SCIP as a monokl output format now** — SCIP's schema has no honest place for Heuristic-tier results, and real non-Sourcegraph adoption is still limited to a handful of well-resourced orgs.</result>

## 1. Schema (primary source: `scip.proto`, fetched directly from the repo)

Core messages, verified from the actual `.proto` file ([scip.proto](https://github.com/sourcegraph/scip/blob/main/scip.proto)):

- **`Index`**: `metadata`, `repeated Document documents`, `repeated SymbolInformation external_symbols` (for symbols referenced but defined outside this index).
- **`Document`**: `language`, `relative_path` (root-relative, canonical, `/`-separated), `repeated Occurrence occurrences`, `repeated SymbolInformation symbols`, optional `text`, `position_encoding`.
- **`SymbolInformation`**: `symbol` (string), `documentation[]`, `relationships[]`, `kind` (a 110+-value enum: Class/Trait/Struct/Method/… with language-specific entries like Rust's `Trait`/`TraitMethod`), `display_name`, `signature_documentation`, `enclosing_symbol`.
- **`Occurrence`**: a range (typed `SingleLineRange`/`MultiLineRange` oneof, superseding a deprecated packed-int encoding), `symbol`, `symbol_roles` (bitset: Definition/Import/WriteAccess/ReadAccess/Generated/Test/ForwardDefinition), `syntax_kind`, `diagnostics[]`, `enclosing_range`.
- **`Relationship`**: `symbol`, plus four booleans (`is_reference`, `is_implementation`, `is_type_definition`, `is_definition`).

Notably, there is **no confidence/precision field anywhere** — SCIP has nothing analogous to monokl's `CapabilityPrecision`.

## 2. Moniker grammar

Verbatim from `scip.proto`: `<symbol> ::= <scheme> ' ' <package> ' ' (<descriptor>)+ | 'local ' <local-id>`, `<package> ::= <manager> ' ' <package-name> ' ' <version>`, with descriptors for namespace(`/`), type(`#`), term(`.`), method(`(disambiguator).`), type-parameter(`[]`), parameter(`()`), meta(`:`), macro(`!`). Crucially, `manager`/`package-name`/`version` each explicitly permit `.` as an "empty" placeholder. Real managers in practice: `npm` (scip-typescript), `maven` (scip-java/scip-semanticdb, per [scip-java docs](https://github.com/sourcegraph/scip-java/blob/main/docs/design.md)).

**Fit for monokl**: less baggage than it first looks — package resolution isn't mandatory (`.` placeholders exist precisely for this). But the full grammar (backtick-escaping, method disambiguators, suffix taxonomy) is real string-parsing surface that buys monokl nothing over its existing `(FileIdx, usize)`/name-string keys, which are cheaper and don't need serialization rules at all.

## 3. Relationship — real vs. paper

The proto's own worked example (TypeScript `Animal`/`Dog`) shows exactly monokl's trait-impl use case: `Dog#` gets `relationships = [{symbol: "Animal#", is_implementation: true}]`. On paper this generalizes cleanly to Override/TypeOf/Reference kinds beyond just trait-impls.

**But**: I checked the actual Rust producer. In `rust-analyzer`'s SCIP CLI (`crates/rust-analyzer/src/cli/scip.rs`, `compute_symbol_info`, fetched from `rust-lang/rust-analyzer` master), the field is hardcoded: `relationships: Vec::new()`. Today's rust-analyzer SCIP output carries **zero** implementation/override relationships. So for monokl's specific first target — Rust trait impls — there is no real SCIP data to consume yet, even though rust-analyzer is the de facto "scip-rust."

## 4. Indexer maturity

- **scip-typescript** ([repo](https://github.com/sourcegraph/scip-typescript)): active — v0.4.0 released Oct 2025, 327 commits, 18 releases, 10 open issues/44 PRs.
- **scip-python** ([repo](https://github.com/sourcegraph/scip-python)): a pyright fork with "no substantial changes to pyright library," developed on its `scip` branch; recent v0.6.3 fixed an inheritance/decorator crash and a macOS zero-document bug — maintained, narrower team.
- **scip-java** ([repo](https://github.com/sourcegraph/scip-java)): javac/scalac compiler-plugin based, covers Java/Scala/Kotlin (with [scip-kotlin](https://github.com/sourcegraph/scip-kotlin)); 775 commits, 30 contributors per [Scaladex](https://index.scala-lang.org/sourcegraph/scip-java), PR activity through Sept–Oct 2025 — the most heavily invested indexer.
- **scip-go** ([repo](https://github.com/sourcegraph/scip-go)): exists, actively maintained.
- **scip-rust**: no standalone project; `rust-analyzer scip <path> --output index.scip` is the built-in indexer, listed in SCIP's own README under "Tools using SCIP."
- **Governance**: as of March 2026 Sourcegraph transitioned SCIP to independent governance — a Core Steering Committee with Meta and Uber engineers alongside Sourcegraph, plus a formal SEP RFC process ([announcement](https://sourcegraph.com/blog/the-future-of-scip)) — real cross-org backing, not vaporware.

## 5. Consumption precedent, and Rust cost

Sourcegraph's own model is **CI-precomputed, not live**: indexers run in CI, emit `index.scip`, then `src code-intel upload`/`src lsif upload` pushes it once ([docs](https://docs.sourcegraph.com/code_navigation/how-to/adding_lsif_to_workflows)). Real third-party consumption exists: **Meta's Glean** ingests Sourcegraph's scip-python output via a cargo-installable "scip-to-glean" converter rather than writing its own Python semantic indexer ([Glean docs](https://glean.software/docs/indexer/scip-python/); [engineering.fb.com](https://engineering.fb.com/2024/12/19/developer-tools/glean-open-source-code-indexing/)). **Mozilla's Searchfox** (mozsearch) consumes scip-java for Java/Kotlin support alongside its own from-scratch indexer ([PR #667](https://github.com/mozsearch/mozsearch/pull/667); [KDAB](https://www.kdab.com/searchfox-improvements/)). Both are genuine "consume SCIP as a supplementary source" precedents, not just theory.

Rust cost is low: an official `scip` crate (v0.9.0, Apache-2.0, [crates.io](https://crates.io/crates/scip)) lives in the SCIP repo's `bindings/rust`, with a single real dependency, `protobuf = "=3.7.2"` (confirmed from its `Cargo.toml`). Parsing is trivial; the hard part is semantic merging — mapping `relative_path`→`FileIdx` and SCIP symbol strings→monokl's local identity, plus reconciling two incompatible `kind`/precision models.

## 6. Should monokl emit SCIP?

Adoption outside Sourcegraph/Meta/Mozilla is thin: **GitLab still has no native SCIP support**, only a conversion-to-LSIF path, despite an open feature request ([issue #412981](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/issues/412981)). Every real producer/consumer pair found is a heavyweight, compiler-backed indexer (javac, pyright, tsc, rustc). monokl's regex+import-binding refs are self-admittedly Heuristic; SCIP has no field to express that, so honest emission means either silently overclaiming precision or dropping low-confidence data.

## Recommendations

1. **Borrow the Relationship shape, not the wire format**: generalize `TraitImplIndex` into an internal enum mirroring `is_implementation`/`is_type_definition`/`is_reference`/`is_definition` on (symbol, related-symbol) pairs. Free naming-compatibility insurance; costs nothing today.
2. **Don't replace `(FileIdx, usize)` with SCIP monikers.** Keep monokl's cheap internal keys; only add a narrow, one-directional SCIP-symbol *exporter* (using `.` placeholders) if/when external interop is actually needed.
3. **Treat `.scip` as an optional, batch-precomputed upgrade path**, not a dependency: add an optional reader (via the `scip` crate) that, when a `.scip` file already exists in-repo, promotes matching occurrences from Heuristic to Structural/Exact — but don't invoke `rust-analyzer scip` live, and don't expect it to solve trait-impls yet (it emits no relationships today).
4. **Don't emit SCIP as a monokl output format now** — SCIP's schema has no honest place for Heuristic-tier results, and real non-Sourcegraph adoption is still limited to a handful of well-resourced orgs.</result>

Full verdict: borrow the `Relationship` shape (is_implementation/is_type_definition/is_reference/is_definition) for `TraitImplIndex` internally, don't adopt SCIP monikers as the identity scheme, treat `.scip` as an optional batch-precomputed upgrade path (via the official `scip` Rust crate) rather than a dependency, and don't emit SCIP as an output format — real third-party consumption (Meta's Glean, Mozilla's Searchfox) exists but is thin outside a few well-resourced orgs, and SCIP has no field for Heuristic-tier honesty. input.prompt:
You're researching prior art for "monokl," a Rust crate that does AST-aware semantic code search for AI coding agents. You have no other context from any prior conversation — everything you need is below. Do genuinely deep research: fetch and read real source/docs, don't rely on marketing copy or your own memory of what these tools "probably do."

## Background on monokl's actual problem

monokl has a per-language `LanguageAnalyzer` trait (one impl per language: TypeScript via OXC, Rust via ra_ap_syntax, Python via tree-sitter-python, Go via a native Rust parser called gosyn, Java via tree-sitter-java) that produces owned `FileAnalysis` structs, later folded by a `WorkspaceEnricher` into a workspace-wide `ImportGraph` + `SymbolIndex`. Every analyzer reports resolution quality per-operation via a `CapabilityPrecision` enum: `Unsupported < Heuristic < Structural < Exact`.

The recurring pain point across every language is **name/reference resolution without a full type-checker**:
- TypeScript: currently regex/AST-pattern heuristics; `oxc_semantic` (scope-aware reference resolution) has been recommended as an addition but not yet decided on.
- Rust: a hand-written heuristic module-path walker (no real name resolution — `ra_ap_hir`/Salsa would give real resolution but requires a daemon process, which was explicitly rejected as too heavyweight for a per-invocation CLI tool).
- Python/Go/Java: no real resolution tier planned yet beyond heuristics — this is an acknowledged gap.

monokl explicitly does NOT want: a persistent daemon, a full type-checker per language, or Salsa-style incremental computation (all considered and rejected/deferred as a separate "independent investigation track" — not because they're bad ideas, but because they're a much bigger commitment than a lightweight CLI tool should require).

## What to research

GitHub's `stack-graphs` (https://github.com/github/stack-graphs) + `tree-sitter-graph`. This is a Rust library purpose-built for scope-based name resolution across languages, without needing a full type-checker — which sounds like it directly targets monokl's exact gap. Investigate for real, with primary sources:

1. **How it actually works**: the core algorithm (graph-based/"stack graph" scope resolution — read the actual paper/docs, not just the README tagline). What's the theoretical grounding (it's based on scope graphs research — find the actual paper(s) it derives from, e.g. Eelco Visser's scope graphs work, and cite them).
2. **What it costs to adopt**: is it a real, importable Rust crate (check crates.io / the actual repo structure)? What's the API surface for defining a language's scoping rules (`tree-sitter-graph` DSL — read real examples from the repo, e.g. the TypeScript or Python stack-graphs definitions if they exist)? How much work is a full language definition — is it comparable effort to hand-writing a heuristic resolver, or genuinely less?
3. **Per-language maturity**: which languages already have real, maintained stack-graphs definitions (check github/stack-graphs and related repos like github/semantic for what's actually shipped vs. experimental/abandoned). Is there real production usage — GitHub's own code navigation feature is supposed to use this; verify that's true and find out which languages it actually covers in production today.
4. **Precision model fit**: does stack-graphs have any notion of confidence/precision tiers, or is resolution binary (found/not found)? How would it map onto monokl's `CapabilityPrecision::Structural` vs `Exact` distinction?
5. **Is this a better general answer than solving resolution per-language?** Be honest about the tradeoff — is stack-graphs itself effectively "write a per-language DSL definition" (i.e., still per-language work, just in a different DSL rather than hand-rolled Rust), or does it give something qualitatively cheaper? Is the project actively maintained (check commit recency, issue/PR activity, whether GitHub itself still invests in it)?

## Output

End with a clear verdict: should monokl adopt stack-graphs (for which languages, if not all), evaluate it further before deciding, or skip it — and why, in concrete terms tied to what you found (not generic pros/cons). Cite real sources (repo files, docs, papers) for every substantive claim. Target roughly 500-800 words.

input.name: research-ast-grep
input.prompt:
You're researching prior art for "monokl," a Rust crate that does AST-aware semantic code search for AI coding agents. You have no other context from any prior conversation — everything you need is below.

IMPORTANT: this must be genuine deep code reading, not a shallow pass. In a prior research round on a different competitor ("codegraph"), a shallow single-pass review was explicitly rejected by the project owner as insufficient — they wanted actual code comprehension, not "search for keywords and summarize what comes up." Apply that same bar here: clone the actual repo, read real source files end to end for the core matching engine, don't just read the README and a few grep hits.

## Background on monokl's actual design (for comparison)

monokl has its own boolean query language for code search: a query parser/lexer/plan (`query/` module) that supports boolean term combination, canonicalization, a text-prefilter stage (via `grep-searcher`) before AST-level evaluation, then BM25-style ranking (K1=1.5, B=0.5) with node-type/coverage boosts, block-level dedup (>50% line overlap), and a token-budget-aware output stage (tiktoken o200k_base, 2MB cap). It also has an `InspectEntry` classifier and a `patterns`/`schema` command family (Part 2 of its spec) for structural pattern matching. Language support is dispatched via an `AnalyzerRegistry` — one `LanguageAnalyzer` impl per language (TypeScript via OXC — a native Rust AST parser, not tree-sitter; Rust via ra_ap_syntax; Python/Java via tree-sitter). monokl explicitly rejected adopting tree-sitter for TS/JS (uses OXC instead) — this is a settled, documented decision, not open for reconsideration; you don't need to relitigate it, just keep it in mind as context.

## What to research: ast-grep (https://ast-grep.github.io/, code at https://github.com/ast-grep/ast-grep)

This is described as the closest architectural sibling to monokl of anything examined so far (closer than codegraph, which is TypeScript-based) — it's Rust-native and tree-sitter-based structural search with its own query DSL. Deep-dive:

1. **Query language design**: read the actual grammar/parser for its pattern syntax (the `$META_VAR` pattern-matching DSL) and its YAML rule format (relational/composite rules — `inside`, `has`, `follows`, `precedes`, etc.). How is a pattern compiled into something matchable against a tree-sitter CST? Read the actual matching engine source (likely in a `core` or `matcher` crate within the ast-grep workspace).
2. **Multi-language architecture**: how does ast-grep plug in a new language? Is it purely "point at a tree-sitter grammar crate," or is there additional per-language configuration/metadata required (node-kind mappings, meta-variable extraction rules, etc.)? How does it handle languages with comparatively little investment/tooling maturity — is there a real quality gap between its flagship languages and its long-tail ones? Look at the actual crate/module structure for language registration.
3. **How does it rank/return results** for a match — is there anything like BM25/relevance scoring, or is it purely structural match/no-match? This is a direct comparison point against monokl's ranking pipeline.
4. **Performance architecture**: how does it scale across a large repo — parallelism model (rayon? something else?), incremental re-parsing, caching. Compare directly against what you'd expect from monokl's two-tier cache (mtime/size fast path -> blake3 content hash fallback).
5. **What's genuinely good here that monokl should learn from or adopt**, and what's a legitimate difference given monokl does semantic/text-ranked search rather than purely structural pattern match? Don't just praise it — be specific about where monokl's design is already ahead (e.g. relevance ranking, BM25, dedup, token budgeting are things ast-grep doesn't attempt at all) vs. where ast-grep's query DSL or multi-language plumbing is more mature/elegant than monokl's current design.

## Output

A concrete comparison with specifics (function/module names, real code excerpts where illuminating), ending in 2-4 actionable recommendations for monokl's query language or `AnalyzerRegistry` design — each recommendation should name the specific monokl spec area it'd affect (query/ module, patterns/schema command, AnalyzerRegistry). Cite real files/lines from the ast-grep repo. Target 700-1000 words.

input.prompt:
You're researching prior art for "monokl," a Rust crate that does AST-aware semantic code search for AI coding agents. You have no other context from any prior conversation — everything you need is below.

## Background

monokl's spec (Part 2 of its design doc) includes a `diff` command intended to produce structurally-aware diffs (not naive line diffs) for code changes, to help an AI agent understand what actually changed semantically between two versions of a file. monokl uses tree-sitter for Python and Java, and a native Rust AST parser (OXC) for TypeScript/JS, and ra_ap_syntax for Rust — so it already has real ASTs available per-language; the open question is what algorithm/architecture to use to turn "two ASTs" into "a good structural diff."

## What to research: difftastic (https://github.com/Wilfred/difftastic)

This is a Rust-native, tree-sitter-based structural diff tool by Wilfred Hughes, who has also written notable engineering material on tree-sitter performance tradeoffs in Rust. Research:

1. **The core diff algorithm**: difftastic doesn't use naive Myers line-diff — read its actual source/docs to find out what it does use (it's known for a graph-based/Dijkstra's-shortest-path formulation over an edit graph, plus using tree structure to align nodes before diffing — verify this from primary sources, don't guess). What's the actual computational complexity, and what shortcuts/heuristics does it apply to stay fast on real files (it's known to have had real performance work done — look for issues/blog posts about pathological slow cases and how they were fixed)?
2. **Tree-sitter performance lessons**: find Wilfred Hughes's own blog posts or talks about tree-sitter performance in Rust (search for these specifically — he's written about parsing performance, memory usage, incremental parsing tradeoffs). What concrete lessons apply to monokl, which uses tree-sitter for Python and Java specifically?
3. **How does it align/match nodes across the two trees** before diffing — is there a notion of "this subtree is probably the same as that subtree, just moved" (tree-edit-distance-style move detection)? This is the crux of a good structural diff and directly relevant to what monokl's `diff` command needs to do.
4. **Multi-language support model**: same question as for other tools — how much per-language work is required, and does difftastic's node-kind handling differ meaningfully across languages in a way monokl should anticipate for its own tree-sitter-backed analyzers (Python, Java)?

## Output

End with concrete, actionable takeaways for monokl's `diff` command design — cite real source files, blog posts, or talks. Target 500-700 words. Be honest if difftastic's approach turns out to be overkill for monokl's actual use case (agent-facing "what changed" summaries, not a general-purpose diff tool) — a lighter-weight design might be the right call, and the research should say so if that's what the evidence shows rather than reflexively recommending adoption.

<teammate-message teammate_id="research-stack-graphs" color="blue" summary="stack-graphs research complete: verdict is skip/defer">
## How it works

Stack graphs extend the *scope graphs* framework from Eelco Visser's group at TU Delft (Visser et al.'s work on modular name resolution) with a stack mechanism. The core paper is Creager, "Stack graphs: Name resolution at scale" (arXiv:2211.01224 / DROPS OASIcs EVCS 2023.8). Name binding info is encoded as a graph where paths = valid bindings; resolving a reference is path-finding. The novel bit over plain scope graphs: compound references (`A.foo`) require *pausing* resolution of one name to resolve another — a natural stack operation, hence "stack graphs." Crucially, graph construction is **file-isolated** — each file's subgraph is built with zero visibility into other files — and cross-file resolution happens later via *partial-path stitching* (`stack-graphs` crate's `partial`/`stitching` modules). This is what gives it incrementality: unchanged files are never reanalyzed. (docs.rs/stack-graphs, arXiv:2211.01224)

## Cost to adopt

Real, published crates: `stack-graphs` (0.14.1, published 2021-05 through 2024-12-13) and `tree-sitter-graph` (0.12.0, the generic tree-sitter→graph DSL engine, still published under github.com/tree-sitter/tree-sitter-graph — NOT archived, last release Dec 2024). Defining a language means writing a `.tsg` file: pattern-match tree-sitter node types, emit graph nodes/edges/attrs (`push_symbol`, `pop_symbol`, scope edges), with `if`/`if none` guards for context sensitivity. I pulled the actual TypeScript definition (`languages/tree-sitter-stack-graphs-typescript/src/stack-graphs.tsg`) — **it's 6,297 lines**. That is substantially more code than a hand-rolled heuristic resolver would typically require, and it's write-only-once-you-learn-a-bespoke-DSL effort, not reusable Rust.

## Per-language maturity — the critical gap for monokl

Only **four** language definitions were ever built in github/stack-graphs: **Java, JavaScript, Python, TypeScript**. There is no Rust and no Go definition anywhere in the repo or its ecosystem. So for monokl's five languages, stack-graphs offers real prior art for exactly the ones where you're least stuck (TS) and nothing for Rust or Go, where the pain is worst.

Production usage is real, not vaporware: GitHub's Precise Code Navigation shipped on Python in Dec 2021 (github.blog/2021-12-09) and TypeScript in Mar 2024 (github.blog/changelog/2024-03-14), both explicitly "powered by stack graphs."

**However: github/stack-graphs was archived by GitHub on 2025-09-09** — read-only, "no longer supported or updated," with an explicit "if you wish to continue development, fork it." Last release was tree-sitter-stack-graphs v0.10.0, Dec 13, 2024. So GitHub built it, shipped it in production for 4 years, then stopped investing in the open-source side — no announced successor. (The generic `tree-sitter-graph` DSL engine lives on separately under the `tree-sitter` org and isn't archived, but the name-resolution-specific layer and all per-language definitions are frozen.)

## Precision model fit

No confidence/precision tiers exist anywhere in the docs or paper — resolution is a binary path-exists/doesn't-exist search. The one exploitable signal: ambiguous references naturally produce *multiple* candidate paths (unresolved overloads, dynamic dispatch), while unambiguous ones produce exactly one. Monokl could map "exactly one path" → `Exact` and "N>1 candidate paths" → `Structural`, but that mapping is something monokl would have to build itself — it isn't a first-class concept in the library.

## Verdict: skip, don't adopt

This is honestly still "per-language work," just relocated into an unfamiliar declarative DSL rather than Rust you already control — and the TypeScript definition suggests it's *more* total code than a heuristic resolver, not less. Combined with: (a) zero existing coverage for Rust or Go, monokl's hardest gaps; (b) the repo being archived with no successor, meaning any new `.tsg` work for Go/Rust would be unsupported from day one with no upstream to file issues against; (c) binary resolution requiring monokl to invent its own precision-tier mapping anyway — there's no case here for adoption over the current path.

The one place I'd flag as worth a second look, not a full adopt: monokl could fork/vendor the existing **Python and TypeScript** `.tsg` definitions as a reference implementation or even reused artifact for those two languages specifically (proven, production-tested rulesets, permissively licensed MIT/Apache-2.0) — but that's "borrow a finished asset for 2 of 5 languages," not "adopt stack-graphs as the resolution architecture." Given monokl's daemon-free CLI constraint is already satisfied by stack-graphs' file-incremental design, this narrow option is at least architecturally compatible if ever revisited — but I wouldn't spend cycles on it now.

Sources: github.com/github/stack-graphs (README, archival notice), docs.rs/stack-graphs, arXiv:2211.01224, github.blog/open-source/introducing-stack-graphs, github.blog/2021-12-09-precise-code-navigation-python..., github.blog/changelog/2024-03-14-precise-code-navigation-for-typescript-projects, crates.io API for stack-graphs/tree-sitter-graph, github.com/tree-sitter/tree-sitter-graph, github.com/github/stack-graphs/languages/tree-sitter-stack-graphs-typescript/src/stack-graphs.tsg.

<teammate-message teammate_id="research-difftastic" color="yellow" summary="difftastic research complete — algorithm, alignment, takeaways">
## difftastic research findings

**1. Core algorithm** — Confirmed from Wilfred Hughes's primary source ["Difftastic, the Fantastic Diff"](https://www.wilfred.me.uk/blog/2022/09/06/difftastic-the-fantastic-diff/): after parsing, difftastic converts each tree-sitter tree to a uniform s-expression (`List{open, children, close}` / `Atom{position, content, kind}`, in `src/parse/syntax.rs`). Diffing is framed as **shortest path on a DAG**: a vertex = `(left_position, right_position, parent-exit-stack)`; edges cost less for "unchanged" matches, more for novel/added/removed atoms; **Dijkstra's algorithm** finds the min-cost route = "most unchanged edges." This is fundamentally a **sequential positional alignment** (walking both flattened token streams in lockstep, tracking nested-list entry/exit), not a general tree-edit-distance over subtree identity.

Graph size is O(L·R) (quadratic in token counts) but vertex parent-stacks made it naively O(2^N) in nesting depth — fixed by lazily constructing vertices and capping to "at most two graph vertices per position pair." Biggest bottleneck is vertex construction itself (millions of vertices on large diffs). Mitigations: aggressive prefix/suffix trimming of unchanged regions, and a **fallback to plain line-diff when the graph would be too big**. A* was tried as an alternative router — "didn't see much improvement" over Dijkstra.

A follow-up optimization write-up, ["How do I boost difftastic by 4x"](https://blog.quarticcat.com/posts/optimize-difftastic/), shows the real-world perf work was almost entirely **shrinking the `Vertex` struct** (nested enums → bitmap → pointer-tagged pointer+counters, −8 bytes/vertex), pruning zero-weight-edge chains (15-25% search-space cut), reusing neighbor-vector allocations, and switching allocators (mimalloc→jemalloc, trading ~20% runtime for fewer pathological-case blowups) — net 4x speedup, 23% of original memory. Confirms the algorithm is Dijkstra over a huge lazily-built graph, and that its dominant cost is memory/allocation engineering, not asymptotic algorithm choice.

**2. Alignment / move detection — the key finding**: difftastic does **not** do tree-edit-distance-style arbitrary subtree relocation matching. [Issue #508 "Highlight moved, novel regions"](https://github.com/Wilfred/difftastic/issues/508), opened by Wilfred himself in 2023 and still open/unimplemented, explicitly proposes this as future work ("if a subtree is deeply novel on both sides but exists on both sides, it could be treated as a move"). Because the core graph only walks `(left_pos, right_pos)` pairs in order, a block moved far away in the file just shows as delete+add, not a detected move. The [manual's Tricky Cases page](https://difftastic.wilfred.me.uk/tricky_cases.html) documents related alignment weaknesses: depth-invariant node matching (`(x)` vs `[x]`), punctuation deprioritized in matching, "slider" misalignment on repetitive/flat structures, and explicit non-support for unordered-collection diffing (NP-hard in general, so intentionally skipped).

**3. Multi-language support**: per the ["Adding a Parser" manual](https://difftastic.wilfred.me.uk/adding_a_parser.html), each language needs: a tree-sitter grammar crate, an entry in `tree_sitter_parser.rs` with `atom_nodes` (node kinds that must be treated as leaves despite having children — misconfiguring shows spurious diffs), `delimiter_tokens` (paired delimiters — omitting causes `(`/`)` to be diffed independently and mismatched), and a highlight query; plus a `guess_language.rs` entry for file-extension/shebang detection. 44 languages supported; the process is described as genuinely lightweight, but `atom_nodes`/`delimiter_tokens` are real per-language tuning, not free.

## Takeaways for monokl's `diff` command

- **Difftastic's approach is likely overkill for monokl.** Its Dijkstra-on-a-huge-graph design solves *minimal, aesthetically-good, general-purpose text-level diffs* — optimized for human readability in a terminal, at real engineering cost (the entire 4x-speedup post is memory-layout surgery on a graph search). Monokl's actual need — "summarize semantically what changed" for an agent — doesn't require finding a globally-minimal edit script at all.
- **What's actually worth borrowing**: (a) converting each language's AST to one **uniform intermediate representation** (list/atom) so diff logic is language-agnostic — directly reusable given monokl already normalizes across OXC/tree-sitter/ra_ap_syntax; (b) per-language `atom_nodes`-equivalent config (which node kinds are "atomic" for diff purposes) and `delimiter_tokens`, since monokl will hit the exact same false-diff bugs without it.
- **Skip**: the Dijkstra/DAG shortest-path machinery and its vertex-memory optimization work — that's solving a harder, more general problem (minimal textual diff) than "what semantic entities (functions/classes/imports) changed," which monokl can likely answer with simple top-down tree matching (match named declarations by name+kind, recurse only into matched pairs, treat everything else as added/removed) — closer to a shallow tree-diff than a full edit-distance.
- **Move detection is explicitly unsolved even in difftastic** (issue #508 open since 2023) — don't expect to get "this function moved" for free from any off-the-shelf approach; if monokl wants that, it's a separate, tractable win: hash/fingerprint named top-level declarations (by normalized subtree content) and match by hash across the two trees before diffing, independent of position. That's cheap and gives monokl something difftastic still lacks.
- **Fallback-to-line-diff-when-too-big** is a pattern worth keeping regardless of algorithm choice — monokl's `diff` should have a size/complexity ceiling per file with a graceful degrade path, since even a from-scratch Rust structural differ can hit the same pathological-input problem difftastic did.
</teammate-message>

Another Claude session sent a message:
<teammate-message teammate_id="research-ast-grep" color="green" summary="ast-grep deep-dive: engine, langs, ranking, perf">
Cloned github.com/ast-grep/ast-grep and read the core matcher, config/rule DSL, language registration, and CLI worker end to end (not just README/grep). Findings below.

**1. Query language / matching engine.** A pattern string is parsed by the *target language's own parser* (tree-sitter) then converted into a `PatternNode` tree — `Terminal`/`Internal`/`MetaVar` — via `convert_node_to_pattern` (crates/core/src/matcher/pattern.rs:223-245). So "compiling a pattern" is really "parse it as normal code, then walk the resulting CST." Matching walks goal vs. candidate nodes with `match_node_impl` (crates/core/src/match_tree/match_node.rs:8-55), using a generic `Aggregator` trait (match_tree/mod.rs:18-27) implemented once for the real `MetaVarEnv` and once for a cheap `ComputeEnd` counter — nice zero-cost reuse of one recursive algorithm for both "does it match" and "where does the match end." Ellipsis (`$$$`) handling is genuinely subtle: it clones the aggregator to *probe* the next goal node against each candidate before committing, specifically to stop failed metavar probes from leaking bindings into the real env (match_node.rs:153-182, with a regression test at pattern.rs:346-362 citing PR #2670). A `MatchStrictness` enum — `Cst/Smart/Ast/Relaxed/Signature/Template` (match_tree/strictness.rs:9-16) — is a tunable spectrum from "match everything including whitespace/comments" down to "match text only, ignore node kind entirely." This strictness knob is exposed per-pattern in the YAML rule (`pattern: {context, selector, strictness}`, crates/config/src/rule/mod.rs:199-211).

The YAML rule DSL (crates/config/src/rule/mod.rs) has three tiers: atomic (`pattern`, `kind`, `regex`, `nthChild`, `range`), relational (`inside`/`has`/`precedes`/`follows`, crates/config/src/rule/relational_rule.rs), composite (`all`/`any`/`not`/`matches`→ReferentRule for named+parameterized reusable utility rules, with cycle detection via `check_cyclic`). Relational rules take a `stopBy` (Neighbor/End/until-a-rule-matches) and an optional `field` that resolves to a tree-sitter field ID (`child_by_field_id`) for precise structural targeting, e.g. matching only inside a for-loop's `condition` field (relational_rule.rs:708-717 test). Rules pre-compute a `BitSet` of possible node-kind ids (`potential_kinds`, ops.rs:31-40, rule_core.rs:124-133) as an O(1) filter before running the real matcher on every node — this is ast-grep's only "index," and it's purely a kind-id bitset, nothing text-based.

**2. Multi-language architecture.** Adding a language is genuinely just: pick an expando char (to dodge `$` not being a valid identifier char in that grammar) and point a macro at a tree-sitter crate — `impl_lang!`/`impl_lang_expando!` (crates/language/src/lib.rs:64-148). There is no node-kind mapping layer, no per-language metavariable-extraction config beyond the single char choice. Consequence: rules are **not portable across languages** — `kind: function_declaration` only works for grammars that literally name that node that way, and ast-grep doesn't try to unify this. Quality gap between "flagship" and long-tail languages is real but narrow: Rust (crates/language/src/rust.rs) and Haskell (haskell.rs) have nearly identical, thin test suites (~5-10 pattern tests each) — the language's "quality" in ast-grep is really just whatever the upstream tree-sitter grammar's correctness is. There are explicit workarounds for known upstream grammar bugs, e.g. tree-sitter-typescript's wrong span for unnamed nodes (match_tree/strictness.rs:68-70, citing ast-grep#1419 and tree-sitter-typescript#306) — so grammar immaturity leaks directly into matcher correctness, which is exactly the class of pain monokl's OXC-for-TS decision was presumably trying to avoid.

**3. Ranking.** There is none. I grepped the whole repo for score/rank/bm25/relevance outside of the `transform` module (string-case transforms, unrelated) and found nothing — matches are pure boolean structural hits returned in file/scan order. No relevance sort, no dedup, no token budgeting.

**4. Performance.** Parallelism is `ignore::WalkParallel` (the ripgrep crate) with a classic multi-producer/single-consumer `mpsc` channel (crates/cli/src/utils/worker.rs:118-158) — not rayon (grepped, zero hits). Every invocation fully parses every file that survives the gitignore/glob filter (crates/cli/src/utils/mod.rs:143-144, `lang.ast_grep(file_content)`) — there is no persistent cache (mtime, content-hash, or otherwise) across runs; it's a stateless one-shot CLI. The only pre-match optimization is `Pattern::fixed_string()` (matcher/pattern.rs:188-205: recursively extracts the single longest literal-text child of a pattern) checked via plain substring `file_content.contains(...)` in crates/cli/src/utils/mod.rs:169-172 — but this runs **after** the whole file is already parsed into a tree; it only skips the rule-matching walk, not the parse itself. This is a materially weaker prefilter than monokl's grep-searcher-before-parse stage, and ast-grep has nothing analogous to a two-tier mtime/blake3 cache at all.

**Recommendations for monokl:**

1. **query/ module** — adopt a `MatchStrictness`-style tunable spectrum for the structural side of a query (at minimum a "signature" mode: match node kind, ignore literal text/comments). Monokl's BM25 text layer already handles fuzzy/ranked matching; a strictness knob would let the AST-evaluation stage relax without falling all the way back to pure text search.
2. **patterns/schema command family** — borrow the `inside`/`has`/`follows`/`precedes` relational vocabulary with `stopBy` (immediate neighbor vs. until-end vs. until-a-rule) and field-targeted matching (child-by-field-id). This is a clean, proven primitive for "structural pattern within structural context" that's more composable than kind+text alone, and maps well onto whatever OXC/ra_ap_syntax/tree-sitter field APIs each analyzer already exposes.
3. **query/ module (ellipsis/dedup correctness)** — if monokl's pattern matching ever supports multi-node capture (`$$$`-equivalent), copy the probe-before-commit technique (clone env, test, only commit on success) to avoid metavar binding leaks on failed backtracking — this was a real bug class in ast-grep (PR #2670) worth avoiding preemptively rather than discovering later.
4. **Not a design flaw, a validation** — ast-grep's `AnalyzerRegistry`-equivalent is cheap (macro + tree-sitter crate + one char) specifically because it only does structural match/no-match with no cross-language kind normalization and no relevance ranking. Monokl's heavier per-language cost (InspectEntry classifiers, BM25 boosts) is inherent to attempting semantic/ranked search rather than a gap to close — ast-grep offers no prior art for BM25 boosts, dedup, or token budgeting since it doesn't attempt any of that.
</teammate-message>

content.text:
ast-grep is back, and it delivers genuinely actionable design detail — one more thread outstanding (CHA/RTA/k-CFA literature) before I write everything up.

**ast-grep verdict: real prior art for the query language, none for ranking/caching.** Its matcher parses patterns with the target language's own tree-sitter parser into a `PatternNode` tree, then walks goal-vs-candidate with a reusable `Aggregator` trait (one impl for real matching, one cheap counter-only impl — same recursive algorithm, two uses). Three concrete things worth taking:

1. **`MatchStrictness` spectrum** (`Cst/Smart/Ast/Relaxed/Signature/Template`) — a tunable dial from "match everything including whitespace" down to "match text only, ignore node kind." Monokl's BM25 layer already handles fuzzy ranking; a strictness knob would let the *structural* stage relax without falling all the way back to pure text search.
2. **Relational rule vocabulary** — `inside`/`has`/`follows`/`precedes`, each with a `stopBy` (immediate neighbor / until-end / until-a-rule-matches) and field-targeted matching via `child_by_field_id`. Clean, composable primitive for "structural pattern within structural context" — worth adopting into the `patterns`/`schema` command family.
3. **Probe-before-commit for multi-node capture** — if monokl ever supports `$$$`-style multi-node metavars, clone the match environment and test before committing, to avoid binding leaks on failed backtracking (a real bug class ast-grep hit and fixed, PR #2670).

Everything else is a non-comparison: ast-grep has **no ranking** (pure boolean match, file-order output, grepped the whole repo — nothing), **no cache** (every invocation reparses every file, stateless one-shot CLI, uses `ignore::WalkParallel` not rayon), and its only prefilter is a post-parse substring check — weaker than monokl's grep-before-parse stage. So monokl's heavier machinery (BM25, dedup, token budgeting, two-tier cache) isn't a gap relative to ast-grep, it's solving a problem ast-grep doesn't attempt.

Waiting on the CHA/RTA/k-CFA literature review, then I'll write all four (plus SCIP) into `05-research-and-decisions.md` in one pass.

Another Claude session sent a message:
<teammate-message teammate_id="research-cha-rta-kcfa" color="purple" summary="CHA/RTA/k-CFA literature review complete, verdict: no tier change">
Literature review done, all citations verified via search (not recalled from memory) — authors/venues/pages cross-checked against dblp/ACM DL/arXiv. Ready to paste into 05-research-and-decisions.md as a new §7 (903 words):

---

## 7. Literature grounding: CHA/RTA/k-CFA and points-to analysis vs. `CapabilityPrecision`

Call-graph and points-to analysis is a mature subfield with a clean precision/cost ladder that
maps onto `CapabilityPrecision` (`Unsupported < Heuristic < Structural < Exact`) better than
expected, with one real gap the literature exposes.

**Class Hierarchy Analysis (CHA)** — Dean, Grove, Chambers, "Optimization of Object-Oriented
Programs Using Static Class Hierarchy Analysis," ECOOP 1995, pp. 77-101. CHA resolves a virtual
call from the declared class/interface hierarchy alone: any subtype of the static receiver type is
a possible target, full stop — no dataflow, no reachability, no instantiation check. Fast, purely
syntactic, known-unsound (ignores reflection, dynamic loading, generics-driven dispatch). This is
`TraitImplIndex`'s (§2) shape exactly: it indexes every `impl Trait for Type` from the AST with no
check on whether `Type` is ever constructed — a declared-hierarchy fact, not a program-behavior
fact. `Structural` is a correct label for this.

**Rapid Type Analysis (RTA)** — Bacon & Sweeney, "Fast Static Analysis of C++ Virtual Function
Calls," OOPSLA 1996, pp. 324-341. RTA refines CHA with one extra static pass: track which classes
are actually instantiated (`new`) anywhere in the reachable program and prune CHA's target set to
those. On their benchmarks (7 C++ programs, 5-20 KLOC) this resolved 71% of virtual calls
statically, vs. CHA's much larger over-approximation. Critically, RTA is still single-pass,
non-iterative, and needs no aliasing or points-to information — it costs the same order as CHA,
not the order of a real type checker. That means RTA is not a stand-in for `Exact`; it is a
finer-grained rung *inside* what monokl currently collapses into one `Structural` tier. Concretely:
CHA-shaped = "declared hierarchy says `Type` could implement `Trait`"; RTA-shaped = "...and `Type`
is actually constructed somewhere in this corpus." An RTA-style filter over `TraitImplIndex` —
cross-referencing implementor types against observed struct-literal/constructor sites, already
information monokl's `SymbolIndex` pass collects — is a legitimate, still-`Structural`-cost
enhancement worth recording, not a new precision tier.

**k-CFA** — Shivers, "Control-Flow Analysis of Higher-Order Languages, or Taming Lambda," PhD
thesis, CMU-CS-91-145, May 1991 (formalizing the earlier "Control-Flow Analysis in Scheme," PLDI
1988, pp. 164-174). k-CFA answers a different question than CHA/RTA: not "which subtype could this
be" but "which closure could this call site invoke," by abstracting environments to
k-deep call-string contexts. It is EXPTIME-hard for any static k>0 — Van Horn & Mairson, "Deciding
kCFA is complete for EXPTIME," ICFP 2008, pp. 275-282 — and the blow-up is fundamental, not an
implementation artifact (companion result: Might, Smaragdakis, Van Horn, "Resolving and Exploiting
the k-CFA Paradox," PLDI 2010, showing even k=1 degenerates badly on OO-flavored code specifically
because class-based dispatch, monokl's actual target, isn't what k-CFA's context-sensitivity is
built to disambiguate). k-CFA is the wrong shape and the wrong cost class for monokl: it targets
first-class-closure flow in dynamically-typed/functional code, not "what implements this
interface" or "what does this import resolve to." Tellingly, even IDE-scale JS tooling built for
monokl's actual problem class explicitly avoids it — Feldthaus, Schäfer, Sridharan, Dolby, Tip,
"Efficient Construction of Approximate Call Graphs for JavaScript IDE Services," ICSE 2013, use a
cheaper field-based approximate analysis instead of full k-CFA specifically to hit interactive
latency. Verdict: k-CFA is correctly out of scope; no part of this spec should be revised toward it.

**Points-to analysis** — the two foundational styles: Andersen, "Program Analysis and
Specialization for the C Programming Language," PhD thesis, DIKU, University of Copenhagen, 1994
(inclusion-based/subset-constraint, more precise, worse complexity); Steensgaard, "Points-to
Analysis in Almost Linear Time," POPL 1996, pp. 32-41 (equality-based/union-find, "almost linear,"
less precise). Bravenboer & Smaragdakis, "Strictly Declarative Specification of Sophisticated
Points-to Analyses," OOPSLA 2009 (the Doop framework), show Andersen-style points-to specified in
Datalog scales across a dial of context-sensitivity (context-insensitive up to k-object-sensitive)
rather than being one fixed cost point — the literature's actual answer for what a non-`ra_ap_hir`
path toward `Exact` looks like, relevant to the open Salsa/persistent-daemon track (§4) as a second
candidate design, not just `ra_ap_hir`.

**Recent IDE-scale precedent.** PyCG (Salis, Sotiropoulos, Louridas, Spinellis, Mitropoulos, ICSE
2021, arXiv:2103.00587) — dependency-free static call-graph generation for Python — reports 99.2%
precision but only 69.9% recall, concrete quantified evidence that even careful assignment-based
static analysis without type inference has a real recall ceiling for a dynamic language, directly
backing this doc's own admission (§04-analysis-fidelity.md, problem 5) that Python forward-reference
resolution without pyright is `Heuristic`, not `Structural`. SootUp (Karakaya, Schott, Klauke,
Bodden et al., TACAS 2024) modernizes Soot's engineering (lazy class loading, fail-early
validation) but not its cost model — full points-to/call-graph construction there is still a
batch, whole-classpath operation, reinforcing rather than challenging monokl's daemon/non-daemon
split. No CodeQL/Semmle paper describing an explicit graded-precision model comparable to
`CapabilityPrecision` was found — de Moor et al., "Keynote Address: .QL for Source Code Analysis,"
SCAM 2007, pp. 3-16, describes the Datalog query engine, and CodeQL's public Java/Kotlin call-graph
docs describe one virtual-dispatch-aware resolution strategy with no published notion of graded
confidence tiers. Worth stating plainly rather than implying false precedent.

**Verdict:** no new tier needed, and no change to k-CFA's exclusion. One concrete, low-cost
documentation fix: `Structural`'s definition in §11 should note it currently spans both a
CHA-shaped fact (declared-hierarchy membership) and would span an RTA-shaped fact
(hierarchy-membership-plus-instantiation) if the `TraitImplIndex` instantiation filter above is
ever built — both are real, distinct precision levels in the literature that this spec currently
collapses into one label. That collapse is defensible as shipped (same cost order, same
soundness caveats), but should be named rather than left implicit.

---

Notes on verification: I independently confirmed every paper via web search (title/authors/venue/pages), not from memory — e.g. corrected my own assumption that SootUp was FASE 2022 (it's actually TACAS 2024). I could NOT find any CodeQL/Semmle paper with an explicit precision-tiering methodology — said so plainly rather than forcing a citation that doesn't exist. </teammate-message>
