1	# Research & Decisions Log (pre-implementation)
2	
3	Findings from a competitive deep-dive (colbymchenry/codegraph), follow-on research into ranking,
4	eval methodology, scale targets, and language support (Rust/Python/Go/Java), and a Rust-idiom
5	audit of the verbatim code in Parts 1-4 — run before any of this spec gets built, so assumptions
6	get stress-tested on paper instead of in a PR review. Two compile-breaking gaps this audit found
7	(a `LanguageAnalyzer` trait missing methods it's called with, and four `MonoklError` variants
8	that were constructed but never declared) are fixed directly in
9	[01-core-architecture.md](./01-core-architecture.md) and
10	[03-multi-language-platform.md](./03-multi-language-platform.md) — this log records why.
11	
12	Part of the [monokl spec](./README.md).
13	
14	---
15	
16	# Part 5: Pre-implementation research amendments
17	
18	> Added before any of Parts 1-4 have been built. A competitive deep-dive against
19	> colbymchenry/codegraph (a mature, production multi-language code-intelligence tool) plus
20	> targeted follow-on research were used to stress-test this spec's assumptions before they
21	> calcify into code. Two categories below: fixes already applied directly to the sections
22	> above, and decisions/open tracks that change what future PRs should do.
23	
24	## 1. Fixes applied in this document
25	
26	- **§Python fidelity, problem 5** (type annotation resolution): `CapabilityPrecision::Approximate`
27	  was not a real variant of the enum defined in §11 (`Unsupported < Heuristic < Structural <
28	  Exact`). Corrected to `CapabilityPrecision::Heuristic`.
29	- **§Section 6, `STOP_WORDS`**: added `crate`, `self`, `super`, `dyn`, `async`, `await`, `unsafe`
30	  — near-universal Rust tokens the original TS/Rust-tuned list omitted, found by tracing the
31	  tokenizer's actual splitting rules against real Rust source rather than assuming coverage.
32	
33	## 2. Adopted, not yet implemented
34	
35	- **Add `oxc_semantic` to the `lang-ts` feature's dependency set**, versioned in lockstep with
36	  `oxc_parser`/`oxc_ast`/`oxc_span`/`oxc_allocator` (same version string — no separate
37	  compatibility matrix). `SemanticBuilder::build(&program)` runs against the same per-file
38	  `Allocator` arena the parser already uses and produces a `Semantic` result (scope tree +
39	  symbol table: `SymbolId`/`ScopeId`/`Reference`, real shadowing/hoisting/TDZ-aware binding).
40	  This replaces regex/text-scanned local-usage resolution in `refs`/`definition` with genuine
41	  scope-aware resolution for within-file references — closing the exact class of technical debt
42	  codegraph's own maintainers flag as their worst (a 20+-resolver heuristic confidence cascade).
43	  `oxc_semantic` is file-scoped: it does not replace `oxc_resolver` for cross-file specifier
44	  resolution, it upgrades what feeds into that combination. Output must be converted to owned
45	  data before the arena drops, same discipline as the AST conversion already documented in §17.
46	- **Build an eval harness before further ranking/tuning decisions are made on faith.** BM25's
47	  `K1=1.5`/`B=0.5` and the token-budget defaults are carried over from Probe's prior tuning
48	  (§29) and are unvalidated for monokl specifically. Minimum viable harness: two layers, not
49	  one — (a) a deterministic retrieval eval (RepoBench-R- or CodeSearchNet-style recall@k/MRR)
50	  run on every commit, and (b) a properly-powered agent A/B (model/effort pinned and logged,
51	  ≥5 runs per condition reporting median + IQR, ≥10 repos with a task list frozen before either
52	  arm runs). Report token and dollar-cost deltas *separately*, broken out by cache-read vs.
53	  fresh-input token mix — codegraph's own published cost-savings claim reversed under
54	  independent replication specifically because token/call reductions and dollar cost decoupled
55	  when its context payload shifted from many cheap cached reads to fewer expensive fresh reads.
56	  Cheapest first step: fill in the four already-stubbed `benches/pipeline.rs` criterion groups
57	  (`pipeline_cold`, `pipeline_warm_cache`, `dependents_warm`, `lite_symbols`, §29) — every
58	  cold/warm latency target asserted elsewhere in this spec is currently unmeasured, including
59	  in monokl's own benchmark suite.
60	- **Add worked query examples and a tolerant natural-language fallback** to the `search`
61	  command's tool-facing description. The `+/-/"phrase"/regex:` grammar itself is confirmed
62	  well-matched to how coding agents actually call lexical search tools (every purpose-built tool
63	  surveyed — Claude Code's Grep, Cline, Continue.dev, GitHub's MCP `search_code` — uses
64	  regex/qualifier syntax; natural language appears only as a separate, explicitly-labeled
65	  semantic tool elsewhere, never mixed into a grep-style tool's input). The gap is discoverability,
66	  not grammar: detect question-like input (`where`/`how`/`?`, five-plus words, no `+`/`-`/`regex:`
67	  modifiers) and degrade gracefully to bare-optional-term matching instead of erroring, since
68	  agents will occasionally route full questions to any tool that sounds like "search."
69	- **Add a `TraitImplEnricher` / `TraitImplIndex`** for Rust — a reverse index (`FxHashMap<String,
70	  Vec<(FileIdx, usize)>>` keyed by trait name, pointing at implementor sites) inverting the
71	  per-struct `RustStructEntry.trait_impls: Vec<String>` across the whole corpus. This is the
72	  structural signal that upstream discovery (interface/trait → implementors — controllers,
73	  services, handlers wired through a trait) actually depends on, and monokl's current design has
74	  no such index anywhere. Follows the exact `SymbolIndexEnricher` shape already in this spec:
75	  `update()` pushes one `(FileIdx, decl_offset)` per trait per file; `finalize()` sorts each
76	  bucket by `(FileIdx, offset)` for determinism. `petgraph` was considered and rejected for this
77	  and for `ImportGraph` generally — its `NodeIndex` would either leak as the public handle
78	  (undermining `FileIdx`'s deliberate non-`Serialize` guard) or need wrapping anyway for no gain,
79	  and it pulls in dependencies (`fixedbitset`, `hashbrown`, `indexmap`) for graph algorithms
80	  (SCC, Dijkstra) monokl doesn't use; the existing hand-rolled `FxHashMap` adjacency-list
81	  approach already matches what rust-analyzer's own `trait_impls_in_crate_query` and rustdoc's
82	  implementors-list generation do structurally (a dedicated reverse index built during a full
83	  pass), differing only by the Salsa incremental caching this spec deliberately forgoes.
84	  "Upstream discovery" for a trait `T` then composes three existing/new indices — no fourth graph
85	  structure needed — via a capped BFS: `TraitImplIndex` → implementor sites, cross-referenced
86	  against `SymbolIndex` for usage sites, expanded through `ImportGraph` reverse edges. That BFS
87	  should adopt the same hardening codegraph's own `GraphTraverser` needed in production: an
88	  `FxHashSet<FileIdx>` visited-set checked at enqueue time (not just dequeue), an explicit depth
89	  limit, and a result cap checked at every push site rather than only the loop head. Surface a
90	  cap-hit as a first-class, matchable outcome — extend `MonoklError` with a non-fatal
91	  `TraversalCapExceeded { visited: usize, cap: usize }` variant, returned inside a
92	  `TraversalReport { sites: Vec<_>, truncated: bool }` rather than silently truncating a bare
93	  `Vec`. The same bounded-BFS pattern generalizes to any of this spec's existing traversals
94	  (`dependents`/`imports_of`, impact-radius-style queries) that don't yet have explicit cap
95	  enforcement at every site.
96	
97	## 3. Validated — no change made
98	
99	- **`ra_ap_syntax` stays over `syn`** for the Rust structural tier. `syn::File::parse` fails fast
100	  at the first bad token with no partial-parse mode (the documented pattern is to emit
101	  `compile_error!` and stop); `ra_ap_syntax` is IDE-designed to always produce a tree, tagging
102	  error nodes instead. Monokl searches real working trees — WIP branches, merge-conflict
103	  markers, mid-edit files — where a single syntax error under `syn` would blank out symbol
104	  extraction for that entire file. No published throughput number for `ra_ap_syntax` parse-only
105	  performance exists anywhere (confirmed absent even in rust-analyzer's own benchmark suite);
106	  the error-recovery gap is the deciding factor regardless of the unquantified speed cost.
107	- **`tree-sitter-python` stays over Ruff's Rust-native parser crates** for `lang-py`.
108	  `ruff_python_ast`/`ruff_python_parser` are explicitly disclaimed by Ruff itself as unstable
109	  internal implementation details (still `0.0.x`, "frequent breaking changes" in their own
110	  words) — not a publishable dependency contract. tree-sitter-python's actual open issues
111	  cluster around bleeding-edge type-hint syntax (PEP 604/695), not the decorators/classes/
112	  `__all__` handling the Python fidelity questions above actually need.
113	- **`WorkspaceIndex::build`'s parallel-analyze-then-sort-by-path pattern needs no upgrade** to a
114	  strict sequential-commit scheme. That extra machinery exists in comparable tools only to
115	  compensate for heuristic name-matching resolvers that disambiguate same-named candidates by
116	  database insertion order — monokl doesn't have that failure mode, because `oxc_resolver` and
117	  `resolve_rust_path` resolve each import to a specific file deterministically (no name-based
118	  candidate list to tie-break), and everywhere else multiple candidates can occur
119	  (`SymbolIndex::lookup`, `definition`'s re-export ranking) this spec already sorts on explicit
120	  keys — path, line, re-export flag — not insertion order.
121	
122	## 4. Open investigation tracks — not decided
123	
124	- **Salsa** (rust-analyzer's incremental-computation engine) as monokl's own memoized
125	  query cache, decoupled from any `ra_ap_hir` decision. Real standalone precedent exists
126	  (Astral's `ty` Python type checker, Biome's analyzer layer both use Salsa independent of
127	  rust-analyzer's own queries) — monokl could define its own queries (symbols-for-file,
128	  postings-for-term) memoized on content hash without ever loading a crate graph, a materially
129	  lighter proposition than embedding `ra_ap_hir` wholesale. Worth a scoped spike, tracked
130	  separately from the item below.
131	- **`ra_ap_hir` integration and any persistent daemon/session mode are a coupled pair.**
132	  `ra_ap_hir`'s `Semantics` gives real Rust name resolution and type inference, but needs a
133	  populated `HirDatabase` via `cargo metadata` + crate-graph construction — a cost pegged by
134	  rust-analyzer's own maintainers at roughly 5 seconds per 100 crates just waiting on rustc.
135	  That cost model fits a warm, long-lived process, not a cold per-invocation CLI. Symmetrically,
136	  a persistent index/daemon mode (mirroring codegraph's watcher architecture) only earns its
137	  own cost past roughly 50k files — below that, the current stateless design's per-invocation
138	  fold cost (re-aggregating already-cached per-file analyses into `ImportGraph`/`SymbolIndex`,
139	  not re-parsing) is estimated at 100-500ms at 10k files and 300ms-1.5s at 50k, a small fraction
140	  of the 15s cold-build budget. Revisit both together, after the eval harness (§2) and the
141	  stubbed benchmarks (§2) produce real numbers — not before.
142	- **Over-fetch-then-rerank staging** in the search pipeline is the one ranking pattern with real
143	  cross-tool evidence (Continue.dev, codegraph, general two-stage IR) beyond what §Section 8
144	  already does; a small import/reference-proximity nudge as a minor multiplier is defensible.
145	  Scope not yet decided — do not build a full Aider-style PageRank-over-symbols system as a
146	  primary rank driver on this basis; Aider's own repo-map algorithm has no published evidence it
147	  beats simpler baselines despite being well engineered.
148	
149	## 5. Rejected
150	
151	- **Embedding-based semantic rerank by default.** No code-specific evidence shows it beats
152	  lexical+structural signals for single-codebase retrieval (identifiers matter more than
153	  paraphrase within one codebase), and every tool surveyed that uses it depends on server-side
154	  vector-DB infrastructure — none of the local-first CLI tools examined run it by default. If
155	  ever added, gate behind an explicit opt-in flag; it is not this spec's default posture.
156	  The stronger version of this argument is a decade of established code-intelligence practice —
157	  CodeQL and LSIF/SCIP have relied on exact, compiler/AST-derived graphs rather than embeddings
158	  for precise code intelligence long before RAG was a term. A small, weakly-evidenced preprint
159	  (Chinthareddy, "Reliable Graph-RAG for Codebases," arXiv:2601.08773 — single-author, no
160	  institutional affiliation in this field, unreviewed, n=45 questions across 3 repos, no
161	  independent replication; vetted and found directionally-consistent-but-not-rigorous) reports
162	  numbers in the same direction (a deterministic AST graph answering 43/45 benchmark questions
163	  vs. 31/45 for vector-only similarity, and LLM-generated dependency graphs missing 377 of 1210

168	  more traversal depth than it actually tested. Independent evidence either way against ever

170	  path this spec never considered but is now explicitly closed off, on the stronger CodeQL/SCIP
171	  grounding rather than the preprint alone.
172	
173	## 6. Language roadmap
174	
175	The v1.2 target of C# is dropped. Priority beyond `lang-ts`/`lang-rs`/`lang-py` is now driven by
176	general market reach rather than one company's internal stack. Go and Java were evaluated as
177	the leading candidates; both get a native `Structural`-tier analyzer, but via different parsers,
178	for reasons specific to each language's actual crate ecosystem (checked directly against
179	crates.io, not assumed):
180

195	convention; a structural tool will see phantom duplicate symbols across tag-gated variants of
196	the same declaration). `CapabilityPrecision::Structural`. Tokenizer: extend `STOP_WORDS` with
197	`func`, `package`, `chan`, `defer`, `select`, `range`, `go`, `iota` when `lang-go` lands
198	(`new`/`super`/`interface`/`struct` are already covered by existing entries).
199	
200	**`lang-java`** — no viable native Rust parser exists (`oak-java` and `java-lang` are both
201	single-maintainer, pre-1.0, near-zero organic adoption; no `java-parser`/`javasyn` crate exists
202	at all). `tree-sitter-java` is the correct choice, same conclusion as Python, and independently
203	confirmed by codegraph's own "native, no-WASM" performance kernel — even it compiles
204	`tree-sitter-java` natively via FFI rather than replacing the grammar. Real semantic analysis
205	(JDT/`javac` classpath resolution via `jdtls`) is daemon-only, with documented real-world pain at
206	scale (20s cold completion on multi-million-line projects vs. 1-2s warm,
207	[eclipse-jdtls/eclipse.jdt.ls#3202](https://github.com/eclipse-jdtls/eclipse.jdt.ls/issues/3202);
208	OOM crashes importing 3000+-file projects,
209	[#1469](https://github.com/eclipse-jdtls/eclipse.jdt.ls/issues/1469)) — unlike Rust/Go, there is
210	no established lightweight semi-semantic tier for Java at all; the field is bimodal. Non-wildcard
211	imports (`import com.foo.Bar;`) give an unambiguous textual simple-name→FQN mapping, easier than
212	Go's or Rust's equivalent case — but the majority of real-world Java imports (JDK, Spring, Guava,
213	Lombok) resolve to JAR-only symbols with no local source, a structural wall no non-JVM tool can
214	cross, and one that bites harder in Java than in Rust/TS/Go because idiomatic Java leans more
215	heavily on external-library symbols per file. Worth the same order of hand-tuning investment
216	codegraph put into its own Java extractor (334 lines — its most hand-tuned language after TS):
217	specifically Lombok-generated-member synthesis (`@Getter`/`@Setter`/`@Data`/`@Builder` → synthetic
218	getter/setter/`equals`/`hashCode` nodes), without which Lombok codegen silently breaks call-chain
219	resolution. No Maven/Gradle multi-module resolver exists even in mature production tools (a
220	documented gap, not an oversight) — cap that specific case at `Heuristic`.
221	`CapabilityPrecision::Structural` for same-module declarations and non-wildcard local import
222	resolution; `Heuristic` for wildcard imports, cross-JAR external symbols, and multi-module
223	source-root inference; `Exact` explicitly out of scope (daemon-only). Tokenizer: extend
224	`STOP_WORDS` with `public`, `private`, `protected`, `static`, `final`, `void`, `implements`,
225	`package`, `throws`, `abstract`, `instanceof`, `null` when `lang-java` lands (`new`/`super` are
226	already covered).
227	
228	A related architectural question raised by studying codegraph (which reaches 30+ languages via
229	one generic tree-sitter-walking engine with thin per-language config, versus monokl's fully-native
230	per-language analyzer approach): whether to add a generic tree-sitter fallback tier —
231	`Heuristic`/`Structural` precision only, search/symbols capability without a bespoke semantic
232	layer — for languages beyond this list. Not yet decided; Go and Java themselves do not need it,
233	since both justify dedicated hand-tuned analyzers on their own merits.
234	
235	---
236	
237	result: Six research threads' worth of findings applied or recorded: two direct spec fixes, three
238	adopted-but-unbuilt changes, three validated-as-is decisions, three open investigation tracks,
239	one explicit rejection, and an updated language roadmap. Nothing in Parts 1-4's verbatim code
240	has been rewritten speculatively — additions here are documented as planned work, not claimed
241	as already-implemented verbatim source.

get stress-tested on paper instead of in a PR review. Two compile-breaking gaps this audit found
(a `LanguageAnalyzer` trait missing methods it's called with, and four `MonoklError` variants
that were constructed but never declared) are fixed directly in
[01-core-architecture.md](./01-core-architecture.md) and
[03-multi-language-platform.md](./03-multi-language-platform.md) — this log records why.

Part of the [monokl spec](./README.md).

## 6. Language roadmap

The v1.2 target of C# is dropped. Priority beyond `lang-ts`/`lang-rs`/`lang-py` is now driven by
general market reach rather than one company's internal stack. Go and Java were evaluated as
the leading candidates; both get a native `Structural`-tier analyzer, but via different parsers,
for reasons specific to each language's actual crate ecosystem (checked directly against
crates.io, not assumed):

**`lang-go`** — **`gosyn`** ([chikaku/gosyn](https://github.com/chikaku/gosyn)) is a real, viable
native Rust parser: 152k+ downloads, weekly commits, MIT-licensed, confirmed Go 1.18+ generics
support (`parse_type_parameters`, generic instantiation/pointer types both present in source and
tests). This is the strongest native-parser candidate found across every language evaluated this
session — unlike Python and Java, Go did not need to fall back to tree-sitter. `go/packages.Load`
(real semantic analysis) is daemon-only by the same argument as `ra_ap_hir`: a 20k-package
monorepo took 3m26s cold to load ([golang/go#69523](https://github.com/golang/go/issues/69523)),
and even a warm gopls daemon took 10+ seconds to serve a new client on a 2,047-package repo
([golang/go#48829](https://github.com/golang/go/issues/48829)). Import resolution is genuinely
easier than Rust's for the common case — no macros, no monomorphization, and a `go.mod` module
directive plus import-path-prefix-stripping gives a project-relative directory directly (mirror
`resolve_rust_path`'s shape, but simpler). Two gaps explicitly out of scope for v1: `go.work`
multi-module workspaces (unhandled — root `go.mod` only), and `//go:build`-tag-gated files
(gopls itself cannot auto-detect arbitrary build tags beyond the `_linux.go`-style filename
convention; a structural tool will see phantom duplicate symbols across tag-gated variants of
the same declaration). `CapabilityPrecision::Structural`. Tokenizer: extend `STOP_WORDS` with
`func`, `package`, `chan`, `defer`, `select`, `range`, `go`, `iota` when `lang-go` lands
(`new`/`super`/`interface`/`struct` are already covered by existing entries).

**`lang-java`** — no viable native Rust parser exists (`oak-java` and `java-lang` are both
single-maintainer, pre-1.0, near-zero organic adoption; no `java-parser`/`javasyn` crate exists
at all). `tree-sitter-java` is the correct choice, same conclusion as Python, and independently
confirmed by codegraph's own "native, no-WASM" performance kernel — even it compiles
`tree-sitter-java` natively via FFI rather than replacing the grammar. Real semantic analysis
(JDT/`javac` classpath resolution via `jdtls`) is daemon-only, with documented real-world pain at
scale (20s cold completion on multi-million-line projects vs. 1-2s warm,
[eclipse-jdtls/eclipse.jdt.ls#3202](https://github.com/eclipse-jdtls/eclipse.jdt.ls/issues/3202);
OOM crashes importing 3000+-file projects,
[#1469](https://github.com/eclipse-jdtls/eclipse.jdt.ls/issues/1469)) — unlike Rust/Go, there is
no established lightweight semi-semantic tier for Java at all; the field is bimodal. Non-wildcard
imports (`import com.foo.Bar;`) give an unambiguous textual simple-name→FQN mapping, easier than
Go's or Rust's equivalent case — but the majority of real-world Java imports (JDK, Spring, Guava,
Lombok) resolve to JAR-only symbols with no local source, a structural wall no non-JVM tool can
cross, and one that bites harder in Java than in Rust/TS/Go because idiomatic Java leans more
heavily on external-library symbols per file. Worth the same order of hand-tuning investment
codegraph put into its own Java extractor (334 lines — its most hand-tuned language after TS):
specifically Lombok-generated-member synthesis (`@Getter`/`@Setter`/`@Data`/`@Builder` → synthetic
getter/setter/`equals`/`hashCode` nodes), without which Lombok codegen silently breaks call-chain
resolution. No Maven/Gradle multi-module resolver exists even in mature production tools (a
documented gap, not an oversight) — cap that specific case at `Heuristic`.
`CapabilityPrecision::Structural` for same-module declarations and non-wildcard local import
resolution; `Heuristic` for wildcard imports, cross-JAR external symbols, and multi-module
source-root inference; `Exact` explicitly out of scope (daemon-only). Tokenizer: extend
`STOP_WORDS` with `public`, `private`, `protected`, `static`, `final`, `void`, `implements`,
`package`, `throws`, `abstract`, `instanceof`, `null` when `lang-java` lands (`new`/`super` are
already covered).

A related architectural question raised by studying codegraph (which reaches 30+ languages via
one generic tree-sitter-walking engine with thin per-language config, versus monokl's fully-native
per-language analyzer approach): whether to add a generic tree-sitter fallback tier —
`Heuristic`/`Structural` precision only, search/symbols capability without a bespoke semantic
layer — for languages beyond this list. Not yet decided; Go and Java themselves do not need it,
since both justify dedicated hand-tuned analyzers on their own merits.

## 6. Language roadmap
input.new_string:
path this spec never considered but is now explicitly closed off, on the stronger CodeQL/SCIP
  grounding rather than the preprint alone.
- **stack-graphs / tree-sitter-graph as monokl's resolution architecture** (full research in §7).
  github/stack-graphs was archived by GitHub in September 2025 with no successor, and language
  definitions were only ever built for Java/JS/Python/TypeScript — none for Rust or Go, monokl's
  two hardest resolution gaps. The one definition inspected in full (TypeScript,
  `tree-sitter-stack-graphs-typescript/src/stack-graphs.tsg`) is 6,297 lines — more code than a
  hand-rolled heuristic resolver, just relocated into an unfamiliar DSL — and resolution is binary
  (a path exists or it doesn't), with no precision-tier concept to map onto `CapabilityPrecision`.
  Narrow option left open, not adopted: fork the existing Python/TypeScript `.tsg` rulesets as a
  reference implementation for those two languages specifically, since they're production-tested
  (GitHub's own Precise Code Navigation) and permissively licensed — not worth spending cycles on
  now.
- **SCIP as monokl's symbol-identity scheme or an output format** (§7). The moniker grammar
  (`<scheme> <package> <descriptor>+`) buys nothing over the existing internal `(FileIdx, usize)`
  keys and adds real string-parsing/escaping surface monokl doesn't need. Emitting SCIP is also
  rejected for now: real non-Sourcegraph consumption is limited to a handful of well-resourced
  orgs (Meta's Glean, Mozilla's Searchfox), and the schema has no field for expressing
  `Heuristic`-tier confidence honestly — emitting it would mean silently overclaiming precision.
- **difftastic's Dijkstra-over-a-token-graph algorithm as the `diff` command's core** (§7). It
  solves a harder, more general problem (minimal, human-readable textual diff) than monokl needs
  (a semantic "what changed" summary for an agent) — its own published 4x-speedup writeup is
  almost entirely vertex-memory-layout engineering, not algorithm choice. A shallow top-down

## 7. Prior-art survey: SCIP, stack-graphs, ast-grep, difftastic

Four more tools/protocols investigated for design influence after the codegraph deep-dive, each
via genuine primary-source research (real `.proto`/source files fetched and read, not
documentation summaries taken on faith). Verdicts feed §2 and §5 above; full detail recorded here
since all four were researched as one batch.

**SCIP** ([sourcegraph/scip](https://github.com/sourcegraph/scip)). Read directly from
`scip.proto`: `Index` → `Document` → `Occurrence`/`SymbolInformation`, with a `Relationship`
message (`symbol` plus `is_reference`/`is_implementation`/`is_type_definition`/`is_definition`
booleans) that is a real structural match for monokl's trait-impl use case — the proto's own
worked TypeScript example (`Dog#` relationships to `Animal#`) is exactly this. No confidence/
precision field exists anywhere in the schema. The moniker grammar
(`<scheme> <package> <descriptor>+`, with `.` as an explicit "empty" placeholder for
manager/package-name/version) is more forgiving than it first looks but still buys monokl nothing
over its existing internal keys. Checked the actual Rust producer: rust-analyzer's SCIP CLI
(`crates/rust-analyzer/src/cli/scip.rs`, `compute_symbol_info`) hardcodes `relationships:
Vec::new()` — today's de facto "scip-rust" emits zero implementation/override relationships, so
there is no real SCIP data to consume yet for monokl's first target. Indexer maturity is real and
active for TypeScript/Python/Java (`scip-typescript` v0.4.0 Oct 2025; `scip-java` 775 commits/30
contributors; `scip-python` a maintained pyright fork); no standalone `scip-rust` exists beyond
rust-analyzer's built-in exporter. Governance transitioned to an independent Core Steering
Committee (Meta, Uber, Sourcegraph) with a formal RFC process in March 2026 — real cross-org
backing. Consumption precedent is genuine but narrow: Meta's Glean ingests `scip-python` output
via a converter rather than writing its own Python indexer; Mozilla's Searchfox consumes
`scip-java` for Java/Kotlin alongside its own from-scratch indexer. GitLab still has no native
SCIP support. An official `scip` Rust crate (v0.9.0, one real dependency `protobuf = "=3.7.2"`)
makes parsing trivial if ever needed — the hard part would be semantic merging, not the wire
format. See §2/§5 for the resulting adopt/reject split.

**stack-graphs / tree-sitter-graph** ([github/stack-graphs](https://github.com/github/stack-graphs)).
Extends the *scope graphs* framework (Visser et al., TU Delft) with a stack mechanism for compound
references — core paper Creager, "Stack graphs: Name resolution at scale," OASIcs EVCS 2023.8
(arXiv:2211.01224). Graph construction is file-isolated (each file's subgraph built with zero
cross-file visibility, joined later via partial-path stitching), which is what gives it
incrementality without a daemon — architecturally compatible with monokl's daemon-free constraint,
which is the one point in its favor. Against it: only four language definitions were ever built
(Java, JavaScript, Python, TypeScript — none for Rust or Go), the TypeScript definition alone is
6,297 lines of a bespoke `.tsg` DSL, resolution is a binary path-exists/doesn't search with no
precision-tier concept, and GitHub archived the entire repo in September 2025 with no successor
("if you wish to continue development, fork it"). Production usage was real while it lasted
(GitHub's own Precise Code Navigation, Python Dec 2021 / TypeScript Mar 2024). Verdict: skip: see
§5.

**ast-grep** ([ast-grep/ast-grep](https://github.com/ast-grep/ast-grep)), read end-to-end (core
matcher, rule DSL, language registration, CLI worker — not just the README). A pattern is parsed
by the target language's own tree-sitter grammar into a `PatternNode` tree
(`convert_node_to_pattern`, `crates/core/src/matcher/pattern.rs`), then matched via a generic
`Aggregator` trait implemented once for the real match environment and once for a cheap
match-end-only counter — one recursive algorithm serving both "does it match" and "where does it
end." The YAML rule DSL has three tiers (atomic: `pattern`/`kind`/`regex`/`nthChild`/`range`;
relational: `inside`/`has`/`precedes`/`follows` with a `stopBy` and field-targeted matching via
`child_by_field_id`; composite: `all`/`any`/`not`/named reusable `matches` rules with cycle
detection). A `MatchStrictness` enum (`Cst/Smart/Ast/Relaxed/Signature/Template`,
`crates/core/src/match_tree/strictness.rs`) tunes how literally a pattern must match, down to
"text only, ignore node kind." Adding a language is a one-line macro pointed at a tree-sitter
crate, with no node-kind normalization layer — rules are not portable across languages, and
grammar bugs leak directly into matcher correctness (a documented tree-sitter-typescript span bug
is explicitly worked around in the strictness module). Ranking and caching are both genuinely
absent — grepped the whole repo for anything score/rank/relevance-shaped and found nothing;
matches return in file order, and every invocation fully reparses every file with no persistent
cache of any kind (mtime, content-hash, or otherwise), using `ignore::WalkParallel` rather than
rayon. This is not a gap relative to monokl — ast-grep doesn't attempt ranked/semantic search at
all, so BM25, dedup, and token budgeting have no ast-grep prior art to compare against, favorable
or not. See §2 for the `MatchStrictness`/relational-rule adoption.

**difftastic** ([Wilfred/difftastic](https://github.com/Wilfred/difftastic)). Confirmed from the
author's own writeup ("Difftastic, the Fantastic Diff") that diffing is framed as shortest-path
search (Dijkstra) over a DAG of `(left_position, right_position, parent-exit-stack)` vertices built
from a uniform s-expression form of each tree-sitter tree — a sequential positional alignment, not
general tree-edit-distance over subtree identity. A follow-up optimization writeup ("How do I
boost difftastic by 4x") shows the real engineering cost is almost entirely vertex-memory-layout
work (shrinking the `Vertex` struct, pruning zero-weight-edge chains, allocator choice), not
algorithm choice — A* was tried and dropped for no real improvement over Dijkstra. Move detection
is explicitly unimplemented: Wilfred's own issue #508 (opened 2023) proposes it as future work and
it remains open. Adding a language needs a tree-sitter grammar plus `atom_nodes` (which node kinds
are leaves despite having children) and `delimiter_tokens` (paired delimiters) — real per-language
tuning, misconfiguring either produces spurious diffs. Verdict: the core algorithm is overkill for
monokl's actual need (semantic "what changed," not minimal general-purpose text diff); see §2/§5
for what's still worth borrowing (uniform IR, per-language leaf/delimiter config, and beating
difftastic on move detection specifically since it still doesn't have any).

## 8. Literature grounding: CHA/RTA/k-CFA and points-to analysis vs. `CapabilityPrecision`

Call-graph and points-to analysis is a mature subfield with a clean precision/cost ladder that
maps onto `CapabilityPrecision` (`Unsupported < Heuristic < Structural < Exact`) better than
expected, with one real gap the literature exposes. All citations below were independently
verified by search (title/authors/venue/page cross-checked), not recalled from memory.

**Class Hierarchy Analysis (CHA)** — Dean, Grove, Chambers, "Optimization of Object-Oriented
Programs Using Static Class Hierarchy Analysis," ECOOP 1995, pp. 77-101. CHA resolves a virtual
call from the declared class/interface hierarchy alone: any subtype of the static receiver type is
a possible target, full stop — no dataflow, no reachability, no instantiation check. Fast, purely
syntactic, known-unsound (ignores reflection, dynamic loading, generics-driven dispatch). This is
`TraitImplIndex`'s (§2) shape exactly: it indexes every `impl Trait for Type` from the AST with no
check on whether `Type` is ever constructed — a declared-hierarchy fact, not a program-behavior
fact. `Structural` is a correct label for this.

**Rapid Type Analysis (RTA)** — Bacon & Sweeney, "Fast Static Analysis of C++ Virtual Function
Calls," OOPSLA 1996, pp. 324-341. RTA refines CHA with one extra static pass: track which classes
are actually instantiated (`new`) anywhere in the reachable program and prune CHA's target set to
those. On their benchmarks (7 C++ programs, 5-20 KLOC) this resolved 71% of virtual calls
statically, vs. CHA's much larger over-approximation. Critically, RTA is still single-pass,
non-iterative, and needs no aliasing or points-to information — it costs the same order as CHA,
not the order of a real type checker. That means RTA is not a stand-in for `Exact`; it is a
finer-grained rung *inside* what monokl currently collapses into one `Structural` tier. Concretely:
CHA-shaped = "declared hierarchy says `Type` could implement `Trait`"; RTA-shaped = "...and `Type`
is actually constructed somewhere in this corpus." An RTA-style filter over `TraitImplIndex` (§2)
— cross-referencing implementor types against observed struct-literal/constructor sites, already
information monokl's `SymbolIndex` pass collects — is a legitimate, still-`Structural`-cost
enhancement worth recording, not a new precision tier.

**k-CFA** — Shivers, "Control-Flow Analysis of Higher-Order Languages, or Taming Lambda," PhD
thesis, CMU-CS-91-145, May 1991 (formalizing the earlier "Control-Flow Analysis in Scheme," PLDI
1988, pp. 164-174). k-CFA answers a different question than CHA/RTA: not "which subtype could this
be" but "which closure could this call site invoke," by abstracting environments to
k-deep call-string contexts. It is EXPTIME-hard for any static k>0 — Van Horn & Mairson, "Deciding
kCFA is complete for EXPTIME," ICFP 2008, pp. 275-282 — and the blow-up is fundamental, not an
implementation artifact (companion result: Might, Smaragdakis, Van Horn, "Resolving and Exploiting
the k-CFA Paradox," PLDI 2010, showing even k=1 degenerates badly on OO-flavored code specifically
because class-based dispatch, monokl's actual target, isn't what k-CFA's context-sensitivity is
built to disambiguate). k-CFA is the wrong shape and the wrong cost class for monokl: it targets
first-class-closure flow in dynamically-typed/functional code, not "what implements this
interface" or "what does this import resolve to." Tellingly, even IDE-scale JS tooling built for
monokl's actual problem class explicitly avoids it — Feldthaus, Schäfer, Sridharan, Dolby, Tip,
"Efficient Construction of Approximate Call Graphs for JavaScript IDE Services," ICSE 2013, use a
cheaper field-based approximate analysis instead of full k-CFA specifically to hit interactive
latency. Verdict: k-CFA is correctly out of scope (§5); no part of this spec should be revised
toward it.

**Points-to analysis** — the two foundational styles: Andersen, "Program Analysis and
Specialization for the C Programming Language," PhD thesis, DIKU, University of Copenhagen, 1994
(inclusion-based/subset-constraint, more precise, worse complexity); Steensgaard, "Points-to
Analysis in Almost Linear Time," POPL 1996, pp. 32-41 (equality-based/union-find, "almost linear,"
less precise). Bravenboer & Smaragdakis, "Strictly Declarative Specification of Sophisticated
Points-to Analyses," OOPSLA 2009 (the Doop framework), show Andersen-style points-to specified in
Datalog scales across a dial of context-sensitivity (context-insensitive up to k-object-sensitive)
rather than being one fixed cost point — the literature's actual answer for what a non-`ra_ap_hir`
path toward `Exact` looks like, relevant to the open Salsa/persistent-daemon track (§4) as a second
candidate design, not just `ra_ap_hir`.

**Recent IDE-scale precedent.** PyCG (Salis, Sotiropoulos, Louridas, Spinellis, Mitropoulos, ICSE
2021, arXiv:2103.00587) — dependency-free static call-graph generation for Python — reports 99.2%
precision but only 69.9% recall, concrete quantified evidence that even careful assignment-based
static analysis without type inference has a real recall ceiling for a dynamic language, directly
backing this doc's own admission (§04-analysis-fidelity.md, problem 5) that Python forward-reference
resolution without pyright is `Heuristic`, not `Structural`. SootUp (Karakaya, Schott, Klauke,
Bodden et al., TACAS 2024) modernizes Soot's engineering (lazy class loading, fail-early
validation) but not its cost model — full points-to/call-graph construction there is still a
batch, whole-classpath operation, reinforcing rather than challenging monokl's daemon/non-daemon
split (§4). No CodeQL/Semmle paper describing an explicit graded-precision model comparable to
`CapabilityPrecision` was found — de Moor et al., "Keynote Address: .QL for Source Code Analysis,"
SCAM 2007, pp. 3-16, describes the Datalog query engine, and CodeQL's public Java/Kotlin call-graph
docs describe one virtual-dispatch-aware resolution strategy with no published notion of graded
confidence tiers. Worth stating plainly rather than implying false precedent.

**Verdict:** no new `CapabilityPrecision` tier needed, and no change to k-CFA's exclusion. One
concrete, low-cost documentation fix: `Structural`'s definition in §11 should note it currently
spans both a CHA-shaped fact (declared-hierarchy membership) and would span an RTA-shaped fact
(hierarchy-membership-plus-instantiation) if the `TraitImplIndex` instantiation filter above is
ever built — both are real, distinct precision levels in the literature that this spec currently
collapses into one label. That collapse is defensible as shipped (same cost order, same soundness
caveats), but should be named rather than left implicit.

## 8. Literature grounding: CHA/RTA/k-CFA and points-to analysis vs. `CapabilityPrecision`

Call-graph and points-to analysis is a mature subfield with a clean precision/cost ladder that
maps onto `CapabilityPrecision` (`Unsupported < Heuristic < Structural < Exact`) better than
expected, with one real gap the literature exposes. All citations below were independently
verified by search (title/authors/venue/page cross-checked), not recalled from memory.

**Class Hierarchy Analysis (CHA)** — Dean, Grove, Chambers, "Optimization of Object-Oriented
Programs Using Static Class Hierarchy Analysis," ECOOP 1995, pp. 77-101. CHA resolves a virtual
call from the declared class/interface hierarchy alone: any subtype of the static receiver type is
a possible target, full stop — no dataflow, no reachability, no instantiation check. Fast, purely
syntactic, known-unsound (ignores reflection, dynamic loading, generics-driven dispatch). This is
`TraitImplIndex`'s (§2) shape exactly: it indexes every `impl Trait for Type` from the AST with no
check on whether `Type` is ever constructed — a declared-hierarchy fact, not a program-behavior
fact. `Structural` is a correct label for this.

**Rapid Type Analysis (RTA)** — Bacon & Sweeney, "Fast Static Analysis of C++ Virtual Function
Calls," OOPSLA 1996, pp. 324-341. RTA refines CHA with one extra static pass: track which classes
are actually instantiated (`new`) anywhere in the reachable program and prune CHA's target set to
those. On their benchmarks (7 C++ programs, 5-20 KLOC) this resolved 71% of virtual calls
statically, vs. CHA's much larger over-approximation. Critically, RTA is still single-pass,
non-iterative, and needs no aliasing or points-to information — it costs the same order as CHA,
not the order of a real type checker. That means RTA is not a stand-in for `Exact`; it is a
finer-grained rung *inside* what monokl currently collapses into one `Structural` tier. Concretely:
CHA-shaped = "declared hierarchy says `Type` could implement `Trait`"; RTA-shaped = "...and `Type`
is actually constructed somewhere in this corpus." An RTA-style filter over `TraitImplIndex` (§2)
— cross-referencing implementor types against observed struct-literal/constructor sites, already
information monokl's `SymbolIndex` pass collects — is a legitimate, still-`Structural`-cost
enhancement worth recording, not a new precision tier.

**k-CFA** — Shivers, "Control-Flow Analysis of Higher-Order Languages, or Taming Lambda," PhD
thesis, CMU-CS-91-145, May 1991 (formalizing the earlier "Control-Flow Analysis in Scheme," PLDI
1988, pp. 164-174). k-CFA answers a different question than CHA/RTA: not "which subtype could this
be" but "which closure could this call site invoke," by abstracting environments to
k-deep call-string contexts. It is EXPTIME-hard for any static k>0 — Van Horn & Mairson, "Deciding
kCFA is complete for EXPTIME," ICFP 2008, pp. 275-282 — and the blow-up is fundamental, not an
implementation artifact (companion result: Might, Smaragdakis, Van Horn, "Resolving and Exploiting
the k-CFA Paradox," PLDI 2010, showing even k=1 degenerates badly on OO-flavored code specifically
because class-based dispatch, monokl's actual target, isn't what k-CFA's context-sensitivity is
built to disambiguate). k-CFA is the wrong shape and the wrong cost class for monokl: it targets
first-class-closure flow in dynamically-typed/functional code, not "what implements this
interface" or "what does this import resolve to." Tellingly, even IDE-scale JS tooling built for
monokl's actual problem class explicitly avoids it — Feldthaus, Schäfer, Sridharan, Dolby, Tip,
"Efficient Construction of Approximate Call Graphs for JavaScript IDE Services," ICSE 2013, use a
cheaper field-based approximate analysis instead of full k-CFA specifically to hit interactive
latency. Verdict: k-CFA is correctly out of scope (§5); no part of this spec should be revised
toward it.

**Points-to analysis** — the two foundational styles: Andersen, "Program Analysis and
Specialization for the C Programming Language," PhD thesis, DIKU, University of Copenhagen, 1994
(inclusion-based/subset-constraint, more precise, worse complexity); Steensgaard, "Points-to
Analysis in Almost Linear Time," POPL 1996, pp. 32-41 (equality-based/union-find, "almost linear,"
less precise). Bravenboer & Smaragdakis, "Strictly Declarative Specification of Sophisticated
Points-to Analyses," OOPSLA 2009 (the Doop framework), show Andersen-style points-to specified in
Datalog scales across a dial of context-sensitivity (context-insensitive up to k-object-sensitive)
rather than being one fixed cost point — the literature's actual answer for what a non-`ra_ap_hir`
path toward `Exact` looks like, relevant to the open Salsa/persistent-daemon track (§4) as a second
candidate design, not just `ra_ap_hir`.

**Recent IDE-scale precedent.** PyCG (Salis, Sotiropoulos, Louridas, Spinellis, Mitropoulos, ICSE
2021, arXiv:2103.00587) — dependency-free static call-graph generation for Python — reports 99.2%
precision but only 69.9% recall, concrete quantified evidence that even careful assignment-based
static analysis without type inference has a real recall ceiling for a dynamic language, directly
backing this doc's own admission (§04-analysis-fidelity.md, problem 5) that Python forward-reference
resolution without pyright is `Heuristic`, not `Structural`. SootUp (Karakaya, Schott, Klauke,
Bodden et al., TACAS 2024) modernizes Soot's engineering (lazy class loading, fail-early
validation) but not its cost model — full points-to/call-graph construction there is still a
batch, whole-classpath operation, reinforcing rather than challenging monokl's daemon/non-daemon
split (§4). No CodeQL/Semmle paper describing an explicit graded-precision model comparable to
`CapabilityPrecision` was found — de Moor et al., "Keynote Address: .QL for Source Code Analysis,"
SCAM 2007, pp. 3-16, describes the Datalog query engine, and CodeQL's public Java/Kotlin call-graph
docs describe one virtual-dispatch-aware resolution strategy with no published notion of graded
confidence tiers. Worth stating plainly rather than implying false precedent.

**Verdict:** no new `CapabilityPrecision` tier needed, and no change to k-CFA's exclusion. One
concrete, low-cost documentation fix: `Structural`'s definition in §11 should note it currently
spans both a CHA-shaped fact (declared-hierarchy membership) and would span an RTA-shaped fact
(hierarchy-membership-plus-instantiation) if the `TraitImplIndex` instantiation filter above is
ever built — both are real, distinct precision levels in the literature that this spec currently
collapses into one label. That collapse is defensible as shipped (same cost order, same soundness
caveats), but should be named rather than left implicit.

**Verdict:** no new `CapabilityPrecision` tier needed, and no change to k-CFA's exclusion. One
concrete, low-cost documentation fix: `Structural`'s definition in §11 should note it currently
spans both a CHA-shaped fact (declared-hierarchy membership) and would span an RTA-shaped fact
(hierarchy-membership-plus-instantiation) if the `TraitImplIndex` instantiation filter above is
ever built — both are real, distinct precision levels in the literature that this spec currently
collapses into one label. That collapse is defensible as shipped (same cost order, same soundness
caveats), but should be named rather than left implicit.

## 9. Representative-codebases corpus for the eval harness

The eval harness §2 calls for (deterministic retrieval eval + agent A/B) needs a frozen corpus of
real repos, not synthetic fixtures, to mean anything. Every repo below was independently verified
against the live GitHub API (size, file count via the recursive git-trees endpoint, license,
last-push recency, and — critically — actual per-language byte breakdown via the `/languages`
endpoint) rather than picked by name recognition alone. That check caught two real
miscategorizations in the original proposal: **oxc** and **typescript-go** were initially slotted
under TS/JS on the strength of their subject matter, but both are themselves implemented in a
different language than the one they process — oxc is 84% Rust by bytes (12,217,475 Go bytes were
never the point; wait — oxc has no meaningful Go, that figure belongs to typescript-go, see below),
and typescript-go (the new native port of the TypeScript compiler) is 84% Go by bytes, only ~12%
TypeScript. Both are corrected below to the language they're actually written in — what matters
for this corpus is which of monokl's analyzers gets exercised, not the tool's subject domain.

**TypeScript/JS (`lang-ts`)**:
- **[microsoft/vscode](https://github.com/microsoft/vscode)** — 96% TypeScript by bytes (139.9M of
  ~145.5M), 187,809 stars, MIT, 1.3GB / 16,686 files, active (pushed within the hour of this
  check). The flagship large-scale real-world TS application; every other originally-proposed TS
  pick got reclassified out of this category once verified, so this is currently the sole entry —
  worth treating as a gap if a second, architecturally-different TS codebase is wanted later.

396	fact. `Structural` is a correct label for this.
397	
398	**Rapid Type Analysis (RTA)** — Bacon & Sweeney, "Fast Static Analysis of C++ Virtual Function
399	Calls," OOPSLA 1996, pp. 324-341. RTA refines CHA with one extra static pass: track which classes
400	are actually instantiated (`new`) anywhere in the reachable program and prune CHA's target set to
401	those. On their benchmarks (7 C++ programs, 5-20 KLOC) this resolved 71% of virtual calls
402	statically, vs. CHA's much larger over-approximation. Critically, RTA is still single-pass,
403	non-iterative, and needs no aliasing or points-to information — it costs the same order as CHA,
404	not the order of a real type checker. That means RTA is not a stand-in for `Exact`; it is a
405	finer-grained rung *inside* what monokl currently collapses into one `Structural` tier. Concretely:
406	CHA-shaped = "declared hierarchy says `Type` could implement `Trait`"; RTA-shaped = "...and `Type`
407	is actually constructed somewhere in this corpus." An RTA-style filter over `TraitImplIndex` (§2)
408	— cross-referencing implementor types against observed struct-literal/constructor sites, already

content.text:
**Android** has used Kotlin as Google's officially preferred language since 2019, but a large share of existing/legacy Android code is still Java — which is already on monokl's roadmap, so that's partial Android coverage today, not zero.

**Kotlin** is the stronger candidate of the two by the same "general market reach" logic that already promoted Go/Java over C#: it's not just Android anymore, it's picked up real server-side usage too (Ktor, Spring-with-Kotlin). My expectation, unverified, is it'd land in roughly the same spot as Java — no viable native Rust parser, `tree-sitter-kotlin` as the fallback, real semantic analysis (Kotlin's own compiler frontend) daemon-only.

**Swift** is real but narrower — it's essentially Apple's ecosystem (iOS/macOS/watchOS), without Kotlin's or Java's spread beyond mobile. `tree-sitter-swift` exists, but Apple's own semantic tooling (`swift-syntax`) is written in Swift itself, which would be the first language on this roadmap that isn't either native-Rust or a toolchain-free tree-sitter grammar — a real added-friction point worth weighing before committing to it.

Want me to run the same verification pass I did for Go/Java on both before touching the roadmap — real crates.io/tree-sitter-grammar maturity, semantic-tooling cost, and adoption data — rather than deciding this off general impressions?

## Top Programming Languages

Python, JavaScript, TypeScript, Java, C++, and C# dominate modern software development on GitHub. Nearly 80% of new repositories used just six programming languages.

TypeScript overtook Python and JavaScript as the most used programming language, marking a historic shift. input.prompt:
You're researching a design question for "monokl," a Rust crate that does AST-aware semantic code search for AI coding agents. You have no other context from any prior conversation — everything you need is below. Do genuine research: check real repos/commit activity/adoption signals, don't just confirm a grammar "exists" and call it good.

## Background

monokl has one hand-tuned `LanguageAnalyzer` implementation per supported language, each reporting resolution quality via `CapabilityPrecision::{Unsupported, Heuristic, Structural, Exact}`. Currently decided: TypeScript/JS via OXC (native Rust AST parser), Rust via `ra_ap_syntax`, Python via `tree-sitter-python`, Go via `gosyn` (a native Rust Go parser), Java via `tree-sitter-java`. Each of Go and Java required real, substantial hand-tuning investment to reach `Structural` precision (e.g. Java needed Lombok-generated-member synthesis for `@Getter`/`@Setter`/`@Data`/`@Builder` to avoid silently breaking call-chain resolution).

There's an existing open, undecided design question already on record in monokl's research log: whether to add a **generic tree-sitter fallback tier** — thin per-language config, `Heuristic`/`Structural` precision only, basic search/symbols capability, with no bespoke semantic layer — for languages beyond the hand-tuned five. This idea originally came from studying a competitor, "codegraph" (colbymchenry/codegraph), which reaches 30+ languages via exactly this shape: one generic tree-sitter-walking engine with thin per-language configuration, rather than a bespoke analyzer per language. monokl's own research also separately deep-read another Rust tool, "ast-grep" (ast-grep/ast-grep) — already established finding, don't re-research: adding a language to ast-grep is genuinely just a one-line macro pointed at a tree-sitter grammar crate (`impl_lang!`/`impl_lang_expando!`), with no node-kind normalization layer at all — meaning ast-grep's rules aren't portable across languages, and upstream grammar bugs leak directly into matcher correctness (a documented real example: a tree-sitter-typescript span bug had to be worked around in ast-grep's own matcher).

Real, current, verified usage-ranking data (GitHub Octoverse 2025, TIOBE Index July 2026, Stack Overflow 2025 developer survey) shows **C and C++ ranking very high** (TIOBE #2 and #3 respectively, both above Java) and currently completely absent from monokl's roadmap — a real, data-backed gap. Kotlin and Swift are also candidates under discussion (mobile-concentrated, narrower reach than C/C++). C# ranks highly too but has been explicitly, deliberately excluded from monokl's roadmap by the project owner already — do not relitigate whether C# deserves a bespoke analyzer; you may still note it as a fallback-tier candidate if the fallback tier itself is cheap enough that the earlier "not worth bespoke investment" reasoning doesn't apply the same way, but flag that distinction explicitly rather than just recommending C# support outright.

## What to research

1. **Real maturity of candidate tree-sitter grammars** — not just existence. For C, C++, Kotlin, Swift, Ruby, PHP, Scala, Bash/Shell, and C# (per the caveat above): check actual grammar repos (github.com/tree-sitter/tree-sitter-c, tree-sitter-cpp, tree-sitter-kotlin situation — note there may be multiple competing community grammars for some languages, e.g. Kotlin — tree-sitter-swift, tree-sitter-ruby, tree-sitter-php, tree-sitter-scala, tree-sitter-bash, tree-sitter-c-sharp). For each: commit recency, open issue backlog health, whether it's used by a real production tool (does GitHub's own Linguist/semantic highlighting use it, does Neovim's nvim-treesitter or Helix ship it as a "stable" grammar, does ast-grep support it at claimed-stable quality, does difftastic support it — difftastic's own language list is a good maturity signal since Wilfred Hughes has publicly documented per-language quirks/bugs for the grammars he ships). Flag any language where multiple competing grammars exist and one is clearly more real than the other.
2. **Real precedent for the "generic fallback tier" architecture pattern itself** — beyond codegraph and ast-grep (already known, summarized above, don't re-research those two in depth). Look for other real tools that do "one generic tree-sitter walking engine + thin per-language config" for broad multi-language coverage — GitHub's own Linguist (language detection, not semantic, but relevant precedent), universal-ctags (an older but real multi-language symbol-extraction tool — how does it handle 40+ languages, and what's its real precision/limitation story), Sourcegraph's own generic symbol search (before/alongside SCIP), or any other credible example. What does the actual cost look like in a real codebase that's done this — is "thin per-language config" actually thin in practice, or does it always grow real per-language special-casing over time (look for evidence either way, e.g. issue trackers full of "language X doesn't work right" reports)?
3. **What would a generic fallback tier actually cost monokl architecturally** — cross-language node-kind mapping (or the deliberate lack of one, per ast-grep's precedent), what `Heuristic`/`Structural`-only output realistically looks like for search/symbols without a bespoke `InspectEntry` classifier per language, and whether the existing `AnalyzerRegistry` dispatch model (one `LanguageAnalyzer` impl per language, matched by extension/content) accommodates a single generic impl handling N languages cleanly or would need real restructuring.

## Output

A concrete recommendation: should monokl adopt a generic tree-sitter fallback tier at all? If yes — which languages should launch in it (prioritize by the real usage data above, C/C++ specifically), and which of those candidates, if any, actually deserve the full hand-tuned Go/Java-style treatment instead based on real usage rank (this is the "when does a fallback-tier language graduate to bespoke" question — give a concrete threshold or heuristic, not just a vague "if it's popular enough"). If no — say so plainly and why, with the strongest evidence you found (e.g. if you find real evidence that "thin config" always grows into real per-language special-casing anyway, that's a strong argument against). Cite real sources for every substantive claim. Target 700-1000 words.

input.prompt:
You're researching a design question for "monokl," a Rust crate that does AST-aware semantic code search for AI coding agents. You have no other context from any prior conversation — everything you need is below. Do genuine research: find real published benchmark numbers and methodology, not vendor marketing claims taken at face value.

## Background

monokl currently mixes two parsing strategies across its per-language analyzers: native Rust AST parsers (OXC for TypeScript/JS, `ra_ap_syntax` for Rust, `gosyn` for Go — all pure-Rust, no FFI) and tree-sitter-via-FFI grammars (`tree-sitter-python` for Python, `tree-sitter-java` for Java — tree-sitter's core is C, wrapped via Rust bindings). monokl is also separately evaluating (in parallel research, not your concern) whether to add a *generic* tree-sitter fallback tier to cheaply cover more languages (C, C++, Kotlin, Swift, Ruby, PHP, etc.) beyond its current hand-tuned five.

monokl's architecture: each file gets parsed once per `LanguageAnalyzer::analyze()` call, producing an owned `FileAnalysis` (no arena-borrowed data escapes — a hard architectural rule). Results are cached two-tier: an mtime/size fast-path, falling back to a blake3 content-hash check, with both an in-memory `DashMap` layer and a disk-persisted `.monokl/cache.json` layer (version + config-hash gated). monokl explicitly has **no daemon by default** — every invocation is a fresh process reading from cache, not a long-lived incrementally-updated index. Documented performance targets elsewhere in the spec (unvalidated, called out as needing a real benchmark pass): roughly a 15-second cold-build budget, and an estimated 100-500ms fold cost (re-aggregating already-cached per-file analyses into a workspace-wide index, NOT re-parsing) at 10k files, 300ms-1.5s at 50k files. Critically: **no real parse-throughput benchmark exists anywhere in monokl's own spec yet** — the `benches/pipeline.rs` criterion benchmark groups (`pipeline_cold`, `pipeline_warm_cache`, `dependents_warm`, `lite_symbols`) are stubbed but unmeasured.

## What to research

1. **Real published parse-throughput numbers**, with methodology, for: (a) OXC — it markets itself as one of the fastest JS/TS parsers; find its actual published benchmarks (check its own repo/docs/blog for real numbers and what it's being compared against — full parse, or parse+semantic analysis?). (b) tree-sitter's own documented performance characteristics — where does its overhead actually come from in practice (FFI/C-boundary crossing per node? memory allocation pattern? is a cold full-file parse meaningfully slower than its famous incremental re-parse path, and does monokl's own use case — parsing whole files fresh, not doing live incremental edits — mean tree-sitter's headline "incremental" performance advantage doesn't actually apply to monokl at all?). (c) Any real head-to-head numbers comparing a native-Rust/native-language AST parser against the equivalent tree-sitter grammar for the same language, if any such comparison exists anywhere (e.g. has anyone benchmarked `ra_ap_syntax` vs `tree-sitter-rust`, or a native Go parser vs `tree-sitter-go`, or Ruff's rejected-by-monokl Rust-native Python parser crates vs `tree-sitter-python` — monokl already researched and rejected Ruff's crates for stability reasons, not performance, so a real performance data point here would be new information). (d) `gosyn`'s own published throughput numbers, if any exist.
2. **What comparable tools report about parsing cost at scale.** Three tools were already deep-researched for monokl (don't re-research their core design, only look for performance-specific data you may have missed): ast-grep (already confirmed: reparses every file fully on every invocation, no persistent cache of any kind, uses `ignore::WalkParallel` for file-level parallelism) — does its issue tracker or benchmarks page have real numbers on how parse cost scales with repo size, and does it report meaningfully different performance across its tree-sitter-backed languages vs. any it might special-case? difftastic (already confirmed: tree-sitter-based, has published real engineering work on performance — its bottleneck was proven to be the *diff* algorithm's vertex-memory layout, not parsing itself, per its own "How do I boost difftastic by 4x" writeup) — does Wilfred Hughes's own writing separate out how much of difftastic's total runtime is tree-sitter parse time specifically, as a real data point on tree-sitter's actual share of a realistic pipeline's cost? codegraph (a TypeScript-based multi-language competitor, already deep-researched for its architecture) — did its own performance writeups mention per-language parse cost differences, especially between its "native" fast-path languages and its generic tree-sitter-walked languages?
3. **Practical implications for monokl.** Given real numbers (however imperfect/approximate) from the above: should tree-sitter-backed languages get a different warm/cold cache-tier treatment or performance-budget expectation than natively-parsed languages? Is there a real argument that monokl's own architecture (parse-once-per-invocation via cache, no daemon, no live-edit incremental reparse) means tree-sitter's core "incremental" selling point is close to irrelevant to monokl specifically — i.e., monokl is really comparing raw cold-parse throughput between a C-via-FFI parser and pure-Rust parsers, not incremental-vs-batch? Does memory footprint (not just speed) differ meaningfully between FFI-based tree-sitter parsing and native Rust parsing in ways that matter at monokl's stated scale targets (10k-50k files)?

## Output

Concrete, evidence-backed recommendations for monokl's `05-research-and-decisions.md` research log — real citations (with real numbers where you found them, clearly marked as approximate/methodology-dependent where the source itself hedges), ending in a clear verdict on whether monokl's cache/performance architecture needs any adjustment as tree-sitter language coverage potentially grows, and what real target numbers (even rough ranges) should replace the currently-unmeasured stub benchmarks. If you cannot find real comparative data for a specific claim, say so plainly rather than estimating — the existing research log already has a strong norm of not fabricating confidence. Target 600-900 words.

## Recommendation: adopt a generic tree-sitter fallback tier, but scope it tightly and reset expectations that per-language config stays "thin"

### Grammar maturity findings (per candidate)

- **C** (tree-sitter/tree-sitter-c): 53 open issues, mostly C23/C2y feature gaps and edge-case bugs (cast-vs-binary-expr, macro handling, enum parsing) — no fundamental ambiguity problem. Mature, widely embedded (difftastic, ast-grep, nvim-treesitter). Clean fallback-tier fit.
- **C++** (tree-sitter/tree-sitter-cpp): 62 open issues, and critically issue #74 documents a genuine unresolved grammar ambiguity — C++ statement parsing is expression-vs-declaration ambiguous without type info that may live in headers the parser never sees. Real bugs in typeid, casts, pointer-to-member, defaulted friend operators. Same tooling adoption as C, but real precision ceiling is lower.
- **Kotlin**: two competing grammars. fwcd/tree-sitter-kotlin (187 stars, active, systematically cross-validated against JetBrains' own PSI parser) is the real one — but its own validation suite reports only **61.2% structural match** against the official compiler AST. tree-sitter-grammars/tree-sitter-kotlin is clearly the weaker alternative (8 stars, 14 commits, last commit Jan 2025). Even the "good" grammar has a hard, documented accuracy ceiling.
- **Swift** (alex-pinkus/tree-sitter-swift): mature — 4 years, 487 commits, 26+ contributors, zero open issues/PRs, used by difftastic and nvim-treesitter. Best-positioned "new" candidate technically, but mobile-concentrated reach per your existing framing.
- **Ruby**: official tree-sitter org grammar, 22 open issues/10 PRs, active (~Mar 2026), long production use (GitHub semantic highlighting, difftastic, ast-grep). Solid.
- **PHP**: official grammar, actively maintained (PHP 8.5 pipe operator recently added); split into `php`/`php_only` grammars in 2024 specifically to fix HTML-injection conflicts for Blade/Twig — real engineering investment, mature.
- **Scala**: official grammar but stale — latest published version is a year old and **explicitly does not support Scala 3 syntax**, now the mainstream dialect. Red flag for launch.
- **Bash**: official, mature, low-ambiguity. codegraph's own community explicitly flagged it launch-ready ("mature Bash tree-sitter grammar exists," issue #648). Cheap, low-risk win.
- **C#**: official grammar, healthy (315 stars, 29 open issues, active through Jun 2026), based on Roslyn's own grammar. Your earlier exclusion was about bespoke-investment ROI, not grammar quality — since the fallback tier explicitly skips that bespoke layer, the original reasoning doesn't transfer here. Legitimate fallback-tier candidate.

### Precedent for the architecture pattern

- **universal-ctags** already runs a two-tier model structurally similar to what you're considering: hand-written full parsers for complex languages, plus a genuinely generic, user-extensible regex-based "optlib" mechanism for everything else. optlib is real precedent that a thin/generic tier can work — but it's correspondingly low-precision (pattern/tag matching, no real tree), i.e. it validates Heuristic-only as the honest ceiling for a truly thin tier.
- **Sourcegraph** ships almost exactly your proposed shape at the product level: fast, always-available "search-based" nav (generically powered by ctags + tree-sitter) as a fallback alongside precise SCIP/LSIF nav for repos with real indexers. Credible evidence this two-tier shape is a legitimate, shipped product pattern, not a compromise nobody actually uses.
- **GitHub Linguist** is not real precedent here — it's heuristic pattern-matching + statistical classification for language ID, not AST-based analysis, so it doesn't validate a code-intelligence fallback tier specifically.
- **The strongest and most important finding**: codegraph — the tool this whole idea came from — does **not** actually keep its per-language config thin in practice. Its own architecture docs and issue tracker show real, substantial special-casing per language: Kotlin needs custom nested-property-declaration visiting, Java needs Lombok member synthesis (the *exact* problem monokl already solved bespoke), C# needs generic-unwrapping/nullable-stripping, C++ needs smart-pointer unwrapping, COBOL needs a fixed-to-free preprocessing pass before parsing even starts. Codegraph's maintainers describe this as ongoing, expected growth. This directly contradicts the "thin config" premise the idea was originally sold on — it's aspirational, not descriptive of what production quality actually requires.

### Architectural cost to monokl

Expect the same erosion codegraph experienced: any fallback-tier language that gets real usage will draw pressure for special-casing, and that pressure won't stop on its own — it has to be actively capped by policy (Heuristic-only ceiling, no `InspectEntry` classifier, no resolution beyond textual/structural reference-finding). The minimal-viable shape, following both ast-grep's precedent (no cross-language node-kind normalization) and codegraph's own `LanguageExtractor` interface shape (per-language string-keyed node-type buckets: functionTypes/classTypes/etc.), is a single generic analyzer keyed by extension, internally dispatching to a small per-language config table. That fits `AnalyzerRegistry`'s existing one-impl-per-language dispatch as one additional impl owning N languages — no dispatch restructuring needed. The one real twist: `CapabilityPrecision` needs to be reported per-language-instance inside that one analyzer, not per-analyzer-impl, since C's ceiling (Heuristic/Structural) genuinely differs from C++'s (Heuristic only, given the ambiguity) and Kotlin's (Heuristic only, given the 61% ceiling) — existing analyzers don't need this since each is already one language.

### Launch set (prioritized by real usage data)

1. **C** — clean fit, mature grammar, TIOBE #2.
2. **C++** — TIOBE #3, real gap, but declare Heuristic-only at launch (not Structural) given the unresolved ambiguity; expect it to generate the most special-case pressure.
3. **Bash** — cheap, low-risk, real demand.
4. **C#** — grammar-quality objection doesn't apply to fallback-tier scope; include.
5. **Ruby, PHP** — solid second-wave adds if usage data supports it.

**Hold back**: Kotlin (documented 61.2% ceiling, not a maturity-over-time problem — it's a hard fact about the grammar), Scala (stale, no Scala 3 support — don't ship a fallback that silently misparses the modern language). Swift is fine technically but low-priority per your existing mobile-reach framing — add opportunistically.

### Graduation threshold (fallback → bespoke Go/Java-style investment)

Two-part test, not usage rank alone: (a) sustained usage in the current Go/Java tier (top ~10-12 TIOBE/Octoverse) **and** (b) documented evidence of a structural-precision ceiling analogous to Java's Lombok problem — i.e., idioms common enough in real code that Heuristic/Structural-only output silently breaks call-chain/symbol resolution for a large fraction of real codebases. **C++ already meets both today** — it's the strongest near-term graduation candidate, and worth revisiting for a native-parser bespoke investment (mirroring the OXC/gosyn/ra_ap_syntax pattern) rather than assuming tree-sitter fallback is permanently sufficient for it.

Sources: github.com/tree-sitter/tree-sitter-c(pp)/issues, tree-sitter-cpp#74, github.com/fwcd/tree-sitter-kotlin, github.com/tree-sitter-grammars/tree-sitter-kotlin, github.com/alex-pinkus/tree-sitter-swift, tree-sitter/tree-sitter-{ruby,php,scala,bash,c-sharp}, Wilfred/difftastic languages_supported.html, docs.ctags.io/en/latest/optlib.html, sourcegraph.com/docs precise_code_navigation, github-linguist/linguist, colbymchenry/codegraph (DeepWiki §7.3 Adding Language Support) + issue #648.
</teammate-message>

<teammate-message teammate_id="research-parser-performance" color="pink" summary="Parser benchmark research findings and recommendations">
## Findings (with real citations)

**1. OXC's own numbers** (github.com/oxc-project/bench-javascript-parser-written-in-rust): parse-only, `iter_with_large_drop` to exclude AST-teardown cost, single-thread + parallel, tested on M3 Max/M2/i7. Concrete: `cal.com.tsx` — OXC 3.4ms vs swc 14.4ms (4.28x) vs Biome 18.3ms (5.42x); `typescript.js` — OXC 26.4ms vs swc 91.0ms (3.45x) vs Biome 139.3ms (5.28x). Biome comparison explicitly flagged non-apples-to-apples (CST vs AST). **Tree-sitter is not in OXC's own comparison set at all** — there is no OXC-vs-tree-sitter-typescript number anywhere I could find.

**2. tree-sitter's own performance framing**: no official MB/s or lines/sec figures exist. The closest thing is an offhand maintainer comment in tree-sitter/tree-sitter Discussion #3413: a custom grammar parsed a 6k-line file in ~80ms, Python's grammar parsed 20k lines in ~120ms — presented as "comparable," not a rigorous benchmark. More telling: tree-sitter/tree-sitter Issue #1277 reports a 1.6MB JSON file taking **~1.2s for a full cold parse and ~0.7s to "re-parse" with zero edits**, consuming ~300MB for two trees. That 0.7s no-op-reparse number is direct evidence that tree-sitter's headline incremental advantage has a real floor — it is not free even in its best case.

**3. Root cause of tree-sitter slowness, where documented**: tree-sitter-haskell's 50x speedup (owen.cafe, corroborated by tree-sitter-haskell issue #41 "terrible performance on medium/big files") traced to the grammar's **external scanner calling malloc per-token** — a C-side allocation-pattern bug in that specific grammar, not an inherent property of the Rust↔C FFI boundary. Separately, Symflower's reported 36x speedup migrating JavaParser→tree-sitter (Go host) was driven by eliminating **cross-process/cross-language calls**, which is a different failure mode than Rust-to-C FFI. Rust's `extern "C"` FFI itself is near-zero-cost (direct calls, no marshaling) — unlike Python ctypes or JNI, which do pay real marshaling tax. Net: no evidence tree-sitter-python/tree-sitter-java pay an FFI-crossing tax in monokl's Rust host; if they're slow, the more likely culprit (per the Haskell case) is grammar-specific allocation behavior, discoverable only by profiling those two grammars specifically.

**4. Head-to-head native-vs-tree-sitter, same language**: I could not find any published benchmark of `ra_ap_syntax` vs `tree-sitter-rust`, a native Go parser vs `tree-sitter-go`, or Ruff's parser/RustPython vs `tree-sitter-python`. Ruff's own writeup ("The Evolution of Ruff's Parser") only benchmarks its hand-written parser against its own predecessor (~2x faster, 20-40% overall linter speedup) — never against tree-sitter-python. This is a genuine gap in public data, not something I'm approximating around.

**5. `gosyn`** (chikaku/gosyn, the real pure-Rust Go parser): README has zero benchmark numbers published.

**6. Comparable tools**: ast-grep's own "Optimize ast-grep to get 10X faster" post (10.8s→0.975s on TypeScript's repo, six rules) attributes the win entirely to regex-cloning and `potential_kinds` matching-logic fixes — it says nothing about parse cost scaling with repo size or cross-language differences, despite specific searching. difftastic's "boost difftastic by 4x" (QuarticCat) confirms the bottleneck was `Vertex` construction/memory layout in the Dijkstra-based diff graph (millions of vertices), not tree-sitter parsing — but the post never gives a parse-time-vs-diff-time percentage split, so I can't cite a number for "tree-sitter's share." codegraph's README states ~60 files/sec end-to-end indexing (parse+extract+write, not parse-only), no per-language breakdown despite searching.

## Practical implications / verdict

- **No public evidence supports differentiated cache-tier treatment by parser type on FFI-crossing grounds alone** — Rust-to-C FFI isn't the tax; grammar-specific C allocation patterns are, and that's only provable per-grammar via monokl's own profiling of tree-sitter-python/tree-sitter-java specifically.
- **Tree-sitter's "incremental" selling point is close to irrelevant to monokl's architecture** — this is well-supported, not just inferred: monokl never holds a previous tree to diff against (fresh process, no daemon), so it always pays tree-sitter's cold-parse path, and issue #1277 shows even the best-case no-op reparse path isn't near-zero on larger files. Monokl should budget tree-sitter grammars at their cold-parse cost, full stop.
- **Memory**: the one real data point (1.6MB JSON → ~300MB for two trees) suggests tree-sitter's peak memory during parsing can be nontrivial for large files; no fleet-scale (10k-50k file) tree-sitter-vs-native memory comparison exists publicly. This is worth a targeted monokl-internal check given the "no arena-borrowed data escapes" rule — the transient peak during conversion to owned `FileAnalysis`, not steady-state, is the risk.
- **Target numbers**: I recommend NOT porting any of the above into `benches/pipeline.rs` as target thresholds — none of these numbers are apples-to-apples with monokl's own file mix, and I want to flag plainly that I found no defensible way to convert "OXC 3-5x faster than swc/Biome" or "tree-sitter Python ~120ms/20k lines" into a monokl-specific per-language budget without measuring monokl's actual fixtures. The one directionally useful data point is codegraph's ~60 files/sec real-world indexing throughput (parse+extract+write combined) — extrapolated naively that's ~167s for 10k files, which should make monokl treat its own 15s cold-build target as unvalidated and likely optimistic until `pipeline_cold` is actually run, not as a number to relax the OXC/ra_ap_syntax/gosyn tier by default. I'd recommend the research log state explicitly: **the only trustworthy fix is running `benches/pipeline.rs` per-language on monokl's own fixtures** — every public number surveyed here differs enough in methodology (file size, hardware, what's measured) that none should be treated as monokl's target.
</teammate-message>

30	  — near-universal Rust tokens the original TS/Rust-tuned list omitted, found by tracing the

55	  when its context payload shifted from many cheap cached reads to fewer expensive fresh reads.

61	  command's tool-facing description. The `+/-/"phrase"/regex:` grammar itself is confirmed
62	  well-matched to how coding agents actually call lexical search tools (every purpose-built tool

66	  not grammar: detect question-like input (`where`/`how`/`?`, five-plus words, no `+`/`-`/`regex:`

73	  services, handlers wired through a trait) actually depends on, and monokl's current design has

75	  `update()` pushes one `(FileIdx, decl_offset)` per trait per file; `finalize()` sorts each
