{ "id": "AC-003", "criterion": "A JSON object being deserialized into SearchOptions that omits \"query\", \"path\", \"allowTests\", \"noGitignore\", \"limits\", or \"exact\" fails with a missing-field error naming that field, per AC-002. A \"limits\" value is handled by one of two independent contracts depending on its outer JSON type: a JSON object follows the object-form contract below; a JSON array follows the array-form contract below as an ORDERED two-step procedure, not a classification by array length alone -- element-type checking always runs first and can fail regardless of the array's length, and only once every checked element passes does length determine the outcome. Any other JSON type (string, integer, a number written with a fractional or exponent part, boolean, or null) fails immediately as a whole-value type mismatch. OBJECT-FORM CONTRACT: a \"limits\" object that is itself present but missing one of SearchLimits' own required keys (\"maxBytes\" or \"maxCandidates\") fails per AC-006's SearchLimits-specific missing-field error, not SearchOptions' own. WHOLE-VALUE TYPE-MISMATCH CONTRACT (applies to \"limits\": \"default\", \"limits\": 50, \"limits\": 1.5, \"limits\": true, \"limits\": null, and every JSON number literal): fails with \"invalid type: <found>, expected struct SearchLimits\" for every case except the number-out-of-range case noted below, where <found> is \"string \\\"default\\\"\" for a string, \"boolean `true`\" for a boolean, \"null\" for null, and for a JSON number, one of two forms depending on a three-way rule (serde_json never emits the token \"number\" for any of them): a number literal renders as \"integer `N`\" if and only if it has no fractional or exponent part AND its value fits within i64 or u64 range (0 to 18446744073709551615 unsigned, or down to -9223372036854775808 signed) -- \"limits\": 50 and \"limits\": 18446744073709551615 both render as \"integer `50`\"/\"integer `18446744073709551615`\". Otherwise, if the literal's magnitude exceeds finite f64 range entirely (e.g. \"limits\": 1e309), deserialization fails at parse time with \"number out of range\" before any type dispatch against struct SearchLimits occurs -- no \"expected struct SearchLimits\" text appears in this one case, unlike every other whole-value type mismatch in this contract. limits is SearchLimits, not Option<SearchLimits>, so null is treated the same as any other type-mismatched scalar rather than deserializing to any default-equivalent value, unlike language: Option<Language>, where null is valid. ARRAY-FORM CONTRACT, applied in this order for any JSON array value: STEP 1 (element-type check, always runs first) -- elements at positions 0 through min(array length, 4) - 1 are deserialized in order against their positional field's own type (position 0: max_results: Option<usize>; position 1: max_bytes: usize; position 2: max_tokens: Option<usize>; position 3: max_candidates: usize). The first element that fails its positional type produces an element-level error naming that field's own type -- usize, never struct SearchLimits or Option<usize> -- and this happens regardless of the array's total length, including arrays both shorter and longer than 4: \"limits\": [\"a\", 1, 2] fails with \"invalid type: string \\\"a\\\", expected usize\" (3 elements, but position 0 fails before length is ever considered); \"limits\": [1, -2, 3] fails with \"invalid value: integer `-2`, expected usize\"; \"limits\": [true] fails with \"invalid type: boolean `true`, expected usize\"; \"limits\": [\"a\", 1, 2, 3, 4] fails with \"invalid type: string \\\"a\\\", expected usize\" (5 elements, but position 0 still fails first -- the 5th element is never reached); \"limits\": [1, -2, 3, 4, 5] fails with \"invalid value: integer `-2`, expected usize\" for the same reason. The array is consumed strictly left to right, and the first failure encountered at the lowest element position wins, whether that failure is an ordinary positional type failure or a parse-level failure on the literal itself -- an out-of-range numeric literal is not an exception to first-failure-wins, it IS first-failure-wins, differing only in that its error text names no field type instead of naming usize. An element literal whose magnitude exceeds finite f64 range (e.g. position 1 of \"limits\": [1, 1e309, 3, 4]) fails with \"number out of range\" ONLY when no earlier position (here, position 0) already failed its own positional type check first: \"limits\": [\"a\", 1e309, 3, 4] fails with \"invalid type: string \\\"a\\\", expected usize\" at position 0, not \"number out of range\" at position 1, because position 0 is checked first and its failure wins regardless of what position 1 contains. An out-of-range literal at position 4 or beyond is never parsed at all, since STEP 1 only checks positions 0 through min(length, 4) - 1: \"limits\": [1, 2, 3, 4, 1e309] fails with \"trailing characters\", identically to \"limits\": [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] (STEP 2's surplus-element rule below), not \"number out of range\" -- the out-of-range literal at position 4 is surplus input, never reached by STEP 1's per-element check at all. This is distinct from an integer-lexical-form element merely beyond u64 range within the checked positions, which does reach dispatch and produces the ordinary element-level error: \"limits\": [1, 18446744073709551616, 3, 4] yields \"invalid type: floating point `1.8446744073709552e+19`, expected usize\" at position 1, exactly as any other floating-point-rendered element would, since position 0 already passed its own check first. STEP 2 (length check, runs only if every checked element passed step 1) -- once positions 0 through min(length, 4) - 1 all type-check successfully, the array's length alone determines the outcome: fewer than 4 elements fails with \"invalid length N, expected struct SearchLimits with 4 elements\" (\"limits\": [] produces \"invalid length 0\"; \"limits\": [1, 2, 3] -- all 3 elements type-check -- produces \"invalid length 3\"); more than 4 elements does NOT fail with a length error, because serde's derived visit_seq for this 4-field struct consumes exactly 4 elements and returns without draining the remaining SeqAccess, so the surplus element(s) are never type-checked and surface to serde_json as unconsumed input, producing a trailing-characters syntax error instead (\"limits\": [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] and \"limits\": [1, 2, 3, 4, \"x\"] both fail with \"trailing characters\", identically, since the 5th element's own type is never inspected); exactly 4 elements succeeds, deserializing positionally -- \"limits\": [50, 100, null, 5] deserializes to SearchLimits { max_results: Some(50), max_bytes: 100, max_tokens: None, max_candidates: 5 }, and \"limits\": [null, 2, null, 4] also succeeds (max_results: None, max_tokens: None) since positions 0 and 2 target Option<usize>, which accepts null positionally the same as it does by key in the object-form contract's AC-006 error surface.", "is_error_case": true, "judgment_call": false },

```json
      "finding": "AC-012's three quoted error strings are factually wrong and a test asserting them would fail. The criterion states {\"file\": 5} fails with \"invalid type: integer `5`, expected a string\", {\"file\": true} with \"invalid type: boolean `true`, expected a string\", and {\"file\": null} with \"invalid type: null, expected a string\". Compiled and run with the project's own pinned dependency (camino = { version = \"1\", features = [\"serde1\"] }, per 01-core-architecture.md:3072), the actual errors are: \"invalid type: integer `5`, expected a UTF-8 path string\", \"invalid type: boolean `true`, expected a UTF-8 path string\", and \"invalid type: null, expected a UTF-8 path string\". This is exactly why AC-013 is correct and AC-012 is not: AC-013's \"expected usize\" strings come from serde's own usize visitor and were verified to match character-for-character, whereas AC-012 applied generic serde intuition to a camino-owned type. No prior spec in this project quotes camino's path-deserialize error text, so there was no correct precedent to copy. REQUIRED CHANGE: in AC-012, replace every occurrence of the phrase \"expected a string\" with \"expected a UTF-8 path string\" -- in all three quoted examples AND in the criterion's introductory prose clause, which currently reads \"fails to deserialize with an invalid-type error naming the found type and expecting a string\" and must read \"...naming the found type and expecting a UTF-8 path string\". Four occurrences total. Additionally, if the drafter keeps the array and object cases enumerated in the criterion's first sentence, note that those two render the found type without echoing a value -- verified actual text is \"invalid type: sequence, expected a UTF-8 path string\" for [] and \"invalid type: map, expected a UTF-8 path string\" for {} -- so any example added for them must not follow the backtick-quoted-value shape the scalar examples use. No other criterion requires any change."
    }
  ],
  "verdict_summary": "12 of 13 criteria verified empirically in a compiled crate (camino serde1): all type shapes, E0277/E0204/E0599 compile failures, and serde error texts match source. AC-012 fails -- its 3 quoted errors say 'expected a string'; camino emits 'expected a UTF-8 path string'. Fix AC-012, resubmit."
}
```

Findings #15 and #23 at `07-edge-cases-and-failure-modes.md:50` and `:61` match AC-010/AC-011's quotes character-for-character.

Empirical toolchain run in a throwaway crate with the project's real pinned deps (kept at `/private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-gabe-Projects-monokl/a82f4f80-7822-4785-a872-33c66baeee45/scratchpad/ac008` for re-verification):

- **Compile-time:** E0277 naming `TsconfigMode` in both Serialize and Deserialize positions; E0277 naming `WorkspaceOptions`; a `WorkspaceOptions` derive attempt fails on the `tsconfig` field alone while `root: Utf8PathBuf` is fine; E0204 confirms `Copy` is genuinely underivable; E0599 confirms `TsconfigMode::default()` does not exist; `#[must_use]` emits `unused return value ... that must be used` as a **warning** with the binary still building and running. AC-001/002/003/004/005/006 all hold.
- **Runtime:** camelCase roundtrip, `missing field \`file\``, Option leniency for missing and explicit null, unknown-key tolerance, swapped range accepted as `Some(100)/Some(5)`, `lineStart: 0` → `Some(0)`. AC-009's two-class split is exact: `invalid value: integer \`-1\`, expected usize` and `invalid type: floating point \`1.5\`, expected usize` (also confirmed `5.0` and `5e0` both take the float path). AC-012 is not unclear — it is a precise, testable proposition that tests false. An implementer following it either writes an assertion that fails, or "fixes" the mismatch by hand-writing a custom `Deserialize` for the `file` field to force the generic wording, which would be a wrong structural change driven by a wrong spec. The remedy is a four-occurrence string replacement in a single criterion; everything else in the document is clean.

# Verdict: FAIL

The corrected AC-010 is genuinely fixed — but an independent sweep found a different false comparative claim, in AC-001.

**Verdict file:** `/private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-gabe-Projects-monokl/a82f4f80-7822-4785-a872-33c66baeee45/scratchpad/verdict-SPEC-008.json` (verdict@1, `artifact_type: spec@1`, `retry_count: 0`, 1 blocker, schema-validated)

## The blocker — AC-001

AC-001 asserts:

> "This is a mixed enum: unlike every other enum this project's specs have locked so far (SymbolKind/Visibility/DiagnosticKind/Language, all unit-variant-only), TsconfigMode has one variant, Manual, that carries data."

False on three counts, all locked by SPEC-005:

- **RustPathAnchor** (SPEC-005 AC-008, `01-core-architecture.md:363-369`) is `Crate, Super, Selff, Extern(String)` — three unit variants plus one data-carrying tuple variant. That is *exactly* TsconfigMode's mixed unit-plus-tuple shape, already locked. SPEC-005 AC-008 even records the identical Copy rationale AC-001 presents as novel: "no Copy/PartialEq/Eq, since `Extern(String)` carries a payload."
- **DependencyTarget** (SPEC-005 AC-005) — three data-carrying struct variants.
- **LangData** (SPEC-005 AC-012) — five data-carrying tuple variants.

The blocker entry contains the exact replacement text for both the enum clause and the Copy sentence. Note the spec's own `reasoning` field is *accurate* — it says "first data-carrying enum variant **on a type with no serde derive at all**." AC-001 dropped that qualifier, and that is the whole defect. The genuine novelty is the mixed shape combined with zero serde derive; the three SPEC-005 enums all derive Serialize+Deserialize.

## What I confirmed correct

Everything else. Built a live crate (camino 1.2.5 +serde1, serde 1.0.229, cargo 1.96.0) with all three types verbatim:

- **AC-010 is fixed.** `01-core-architecture.md:1217-1219` does read "an underflow panic is a real possibility, not a theoretical one," SPEC-006 AC-004 does quote it, and AC-010 now states both gaps are documented with *different* consequences. The false contrast is gone.
- **AC-009's three-class rule undisturbed** — all four classes reproduced exactly, and SPEC-007 AC-006 does contain "three rejection classes in total ... not two" verbatim. Its characterization of SPEC-003 AC-012 ("likewise fails to deserialize," no error class named) is also accurate.
- **AC-012/AC-013 undisturbed** — every enumerated case quoted and reproduced, including `sequence`/`map` for array/object. A plain-`String` contrast run returned `expected a string` vs camino's `expected a UTF-8 path string`, confirming AC-012's camino-specific claim.
- Compile probes: AC-002/AC-003 → E0277 naming each type specifically; AC-003's sharper "would fail on the tsconfig field alone" confirmed (root satisfies the bound via serde1); AC-006 → E0599; AC-005's `#[must_use]` is a warning, not an error, and `new` warns not at all.
- Findings #15/#23 quoted verbatim, correctly located in Part 1 (lines 50, 61).
- No TBDs. 8/13 criteria carry `is_error_case: true` with real coverage. Scope is one planning cycle.

## For your decision

This is the fifth defect and the **third of the citation-accuracy class**. The type-shape substance has been correct throughout — every failure has been an unverified "unlike/first/only" claim about a sibling spec. Those claims add no implementable content to a type-lock spec and have now caused three of five defects. This is a mixed enum -- Manual carries data while Auto and Skip do not -- a shape this project has already locked elsewhere (SPEC-005 AC-005's DependencyTarget, AC-008's RustPathAnchor, and AC-012's LangData all mix unit and data-carrying variants), so the mixed shape itself is not novel. What is novel is the combination: TsconfigMode is this project's first data-carrying-variant enum with no serde derive at all -- every other data-carrying enum locked so far (RustPathAnchor, DependencyTarget, LangData) derives Serialize+Deserialize, so this is the first time this project locks what a mixed enum's variants look like without any accompanying JSON contract to describe. No source document states or enforces that ExtractRequest's line_start, when both fields are present, is less than or equal to line_end -- ExtractRequest derives Deserialize with no custom validation and no cross-field constraint carries this invariant, so a JSON object with lineStart: 100, lineEnd: 5 deserializes successfully as-is, structurally identical to the unenforced invariant SPEC-006 AC-004 establishes for CodeBlock's line_start/line_end. content.content:
39:7. **Bad `regex:` term: hard error in one search stage, silently dropped in the next.** Stage 4 builds one combined regex from all terms and hard-fails the whole query (`?`) on any invalid pattern; stage 5 builds per-term regexes for highlighting and explicitly "silently drops regex compile failures." Same input problem, two contradictory outcomes within one command.
40:8. **`+regex:foo` loses more than the comment claims.** The code comment says it "silently loses modifier"; tracing the lexer shows it actually degrades all the way to an optional escaped-literal match on the string `foo` — both the required-modifier *and* the regex semantics are discarded, not just the modifier.
56:21. Exclusion-only queries (`-foo -bar`, no positive terms) always silently return an empty response with no diagnostic explaining that this is a no-op by design.
75:7. `coverage`'s `find_refs` call truncates at `max_refs=100` with no propagation of the existing `truncated` flag into `CoverageResult` — a widely-used symbol whose only test reference falls outside the first 100 can be silently mislabeled `untested`.
76:8. `definition` has no cap or truncation flag on ambiguous matches, unlike `refs`'s `max_refs`/`truncated` — a generic name queried workspace-wide returns every declaration site unbounded.
111:7. Disk-full/permission-denied during cache persistence aborts the entire command via `?`, even though the in-memory analysis that answers the query already succeeded — contradicts the doc's own framing of persistence as a decoupled, secondary concern.
112:8. Unrelated-history merge-base failure hard-errors the whole command rather than degrading to `FullRepo` with a warning, the pattern used elsewhere in this file for precision degradation.
147:7. Associated consts and associated types inside `impl` blocks are dropped — only `fn` items are extracted (pre-existing limitation in Part 3 too, but unaddressed here despite this being the fidelity-focused pass).
148:8. Trait body methods (required and default-impl) are never extracted as symbols at all — only `impl` bodies get per-method extraction.

AC-002's cross-spec novelty claim survived an independent scan of every `pub struct`/`pub enum` in all seven docs.

**Four blockers.** Notably, two are in text the canon-auditor itself introduced — the added material was not executed before being added.

1. **AC-006** — the double-backslash worked example is self-contradictory. Examples 1/2/4 write payloads as Rust string literals (verified correct); example 3 writes `Token::QuotedString("a\\b")` (Rust literal = one backslash) while its own prose says "two literal backslash characters, not one." The observable half is correct; the boundary-safety conclusion does not follow from the false premise.

Compiling the module tree with `ParsedTerm`'s fields private fails with two `E0616` errors, because `plan.rs` reads `t.modifier` and `t.pattern` across a module boundary. AC-002 already sets the precedent by explicitly locking `Lexer`'s fields as private.

4. **AC-019** — "never appear ... **under any input**" is false. Since QueryPlan's fields are `pub`, `QueryPlan { terms: parse("-foo").unwrap(), required: vec![0], .. }.search_patterns()` returns `["foo"]`. And `required: vec![5]` with empty `terms` panics on the unchecked `self.terms[i]` at line 890 — an unlocked panic path in a method `api_surface` describes as total with no `error_conditions`.

        "with an out-of-bounds index, not return an error or an empty result -- e.g. "
        "QueryPlan { terms: vec![], required: vec![5], excluded: vec![], scored: vec![] }"

        "exists regardless of whether the QueryPlan was built via from_terms; the API surface "
        "gives search_patterns() no error_conditions because from_terms-built plans can never "
        "trigger it, but a directly-constructed one can."

        "\"guaranteed-safe by from_terms's own construction\" and \"safe in general\" -- the "
        "public struct's pub fields mean the invariant from_terms maintains is not enforced at "
        "the type level, so this is a real, reachable panic path worth locking precisely rather "
        "than assuming from_terms's own safety extends to every possible QueryPlan value."
    )
}

content.text:
No tests exist yet — this project hasn't reached the implementation stage. Everything so far is spec@1 documents (`.claude/specs/*.json`); no code, no test files. So the honest way to answer your question is in two parts:

**Do the specs themselves cover happy path + corner/error cases?** Reasonably well, and getting more rigorous over time — 149 total acceptance criteria across the 8 gated specs, 40% explicitly flagged `is_error_case: true`:

| Spec | Criteria | Error-case | % |
|---|---|---|---|
| SPEC-001 (MonoklError) | 24 | 17 | 71% |
| SPEC-003 (SymbolKind/Visibility/SymbolEntry) | 12 | 6 | 50% |
| SPEC-004 (Cargo.toml/lib.rs) | 28 | 5 | 18% |
| SPEC-005 (Dependency/export/JSX/LangData) | 19 | 9 | 47% |
| SPEC-006 (result/diagnostic primitives) | 15 | 6 | 40% |
| SPEC-007 (search request/response) | 16 | 4 | 25% |
| SPEC-008 (workspace/extract config) | 13 | 6 | 46% |
| SPEC-009 (query language) | 22 | 6 | 27% |

That 40% undercounts real corner-case coverage, though — plenty of non-error criteria are corner cases too (they just describe *valid* surprising behavior rather than a failure: SPEC-009's whitespace-insensitivity finding, the `Default`-impl-inertness findings in SPEC-007, boundary-literal handling). SPEC-009 in particular (the query lexer/parser — the first genuinely algorithmic track, not just type-shape) went through 3 exit-gate rounds specifically hunting missed corners: multi-byte UTF-8 boundaries, NBSP whitespace divergence, `+`/`-` parity, an unchecked-index panic path. Every one of those was caught by actually compiling and running the code against adversarial inputs, not by reasoning abstractly.

**The real gap:** none of these criteria have been translated into actual test code yet. That's the `vector` (planning) → `lambda` (TDD implementation) phase, which hasn't run for any of these 9 specs. The process is *designed* to prevent silent drops there — `vector-planner` requires every criterion to appear in some task's `covers_criteria`, and `vector-challenger` explicitly checks for orphaned criteria before implementation starts — but that's a designed guarantee, not yet an exercised one. So: strong confidence in the spec layer, zero confidence claimed about actual tests, because none exist.

content.text:
The plan@1 for SPEC-004 is complete, adversarially reviewed twice, and every finding from both review passes was fixed and empirically re-verified against a real `cargo 1.96.0` install — not just re-read.

**File:** `/Users/gabe/Projects/monokl/.claude/plans/PLAN-004.json`

**Summary:**
- 23 tasks (T-001–T-023), dependency-ordered: workspace root Cargo.toml first (T-001–T-006), then the crate's own Cargo.toml section-by-section (T-007–T-016), then lib.rs (T-017), then cross-file consistency checks (T-018 AC-015, T-019 AC-016), then the three remaining behavioral criteria in isolated `/tmp` fixtures (T-020 AC-008B, T-021 AC-001B, T-022 AC-003B), and a supplementary offline structural-parse gate (T-023).
- All 28 SPEC-004 acceptance criteria (including AC-001B, AC-003B, AC-008B) appear in `covers_criteria`.
- `spec_file_path`, `spec_hash` (sha256 of the spec file's raw bytes), and `linked_requirement` (REQ-004) are propagated per the plan@1 contract.

**Key engineering decision, stated explicitly in the plan's `architecture`/`reasoning` fields:** two real, spec-documented gaps — no `.cargo/config.toml [registries.orin-cargo]` entry anywhere in the corpus (AC-008B), and io-errors not existing anywhere in the workspace — make `cargo build`/`check`/`install` against the real crate manifest permanently unresolvable, confirmed empirically (`cargo metadata --no-deps` fails at TOML *parse* time the instant `registry = "orin-cargo"` appears, regardless of network or io-errors). The plan therefore verifies content-locking criteria via offline `grep`/`diff` text-exactness, and behavioral criteria via isolated `/tmp` fixture crates — every expected cargo error string embedded in the plan was reproduced live during planning, not invented.

**Review history:** the first vector-challenger pass found 9 real defects (false-red grep windows, a false-green exit-code bug, a manifest-mutating task that violated the verbatim lock, an under-tested fixture). All fixed and re-verified. A second pass found 4 more (one inconsistent commit step, a systemic cwd-persists-across-steps hazard in 7 tasks that `cd` into a fixture then delete it, 3 remaining pipe-swallows-exit-status bugs on `is_error_case` criteria, and two coverage-attribution/test-mismatch gaps). All fixed and re-verified — final state: every fixture command now runs in a `(cd ... && ...)` subshell so cleanup and commit steps never execute from a deleted working directory, and every exit-code assertion captures `$?` immediately after command substitution rather than after a pipe to `tail`.
